a720u10-jun17-01-i: There were some very strong feelings expressed here but often candidates were at a loss to show the techniques and significant language choices which create these feelings in the reader. Other problems occurred when candidates took an outraged stance against Januarie and then used up valuable time by describing different approaches to women in the 14th and 21st centuries. Others took a great deal of time to get around to Januarie because they tended to “work through” the extract and therefore spent far too long on the first 3 lines which deal with May’s beauty. More effective answers showed in a brief remark how the presentation of May’s fresh and innocent beauty clashed with the language used to describe Januarie’s response to her. There were some splendid answers which showed very clearly how Chaucer has balanced disgust, contempt, comedy and maybe even a little sympathy for a foolish old man in these lines.
a720u10-jun17-01-ii: Most candidates chose appropriate material from the text and there was some secure writing on a number of the characters with some subtle treatment of Placebo, Justinus and Pluto as well as the more obvious choices. However, as in all other part (ii) responses, many candidates did not take sufficient note of the prompt in the question which should trigger AO3 work. In this case social status and ability were the prompts and as only one quarter of the marks in this section can be gained under AO3 it is fairly obvious that candidates should be relevantly focused, economical and selective in their choice of material.
a720u10-jun17-02-i: Some candidates struggled to understand the poem. Very few could unpick the image “poor aspen wretch” and there were many who simply could not understand the basic idea underpinning the poem which is of course a threat to haunt a lost lover but to keep her wondering about the precise nature of her punishment. Once again, the tendency to “work through” the poem without establishing a clear overview hampered some candidates seriously as they lost themselves in over-detailed analyses of word choices and punctuation and lost sight of the range of powerful feelings that were on display. Here as elsewhere in Part (i) responses there was a great deal of sterile feature spotting and “naming of parts”. Candidates must be convinced that there is no merit in the use of technical terminology simply for the purposes of labelling.
a720u10-jun17-02-ii:
The contextual trigger here is “attitudes to women” and the view to be considered is that, for Donne, women are a source of “as much frustration as joy”. Perhaps if candidates had made a note to themselves at the planning stage of a detail such as the view mentioned in the previous sentence it would have helped them to avoid re-hashing John Carey’s and Simon Schama’s recent documentaries on the poet with all their playful speculation upon what John Donne might or might not have been doing/intending when he wrote his verse. Material such as the above, used as a primary study aid for Donne, has produced reams of unsupported assertion about the relationship between Donne’ s poems and his life which contribute
4 nothing of value to a critical analysis of his poetry. Candidates must be convinced that it doesn’t matter who the woman in The Flea might be – if there ever was a woman and a flea – and colourful accounts of the young Jack Donne leaving the Inns of Court to spend the evening with a courtesan in the upper room of an inn are entertaining, imaginative writing but contribute nothing to an understanding of poetic technique in Elegy XIX. Centres who study Donne are encouraged to move their candidates’ attention away from speculative biographical tittle-tattle and back to an objective analysis of the poetry.
a720u10-jun17-03-i: There were some carefully considered responses to Adam’s speech here and what it suggested about the nature of the relationship between him and Eve but some candidates struggled to see the difference between the presentation of a character and the presentation of a relationship. The character’s language, tone and attitude indicate the nature of the character at that stage of the poem but the same things imply a state of affairs between Adam and Eve and that is where the emphasis should have been. As noted above, many candidates could not resist descriptions of Milton’s disappointing marriage and his ideas about divorce which could not be rewarded here.
a720u10-jun17-03-ii: “…the perspective of the fallen world” should have provided plenty of opportunities to write about theological and political contexts and it would have been perfectly feasible to make use of Milton’s writings on married relationships in this section. The philosophical problems inherent in writing about what cannot be experienced but only imagined are at the core of this poem and most candidates saw that there were issues here. The best responses showed how the power of imagination and Milton’s imagery made some aspects of Eden convincing but there remained the issue of transgression growing by stages in the disagreements between the first couple. While many responses were of the highest quality, centres which choose Milton might do well to explore the theological and philosophical notions of sin and free will a little more thoroughly in order to avoid assertive and inaccurate approaches.
a720u10-jun17-04-i: This is a complicated poem with several layers and turns when it comes to the presentation of the powerful feelings involved – awe; fear; false self-consolation; fear; anger; confusion and back to awe. The twin themes of mortality and the classical world are central to Keats’ work and this poem should have felt familiar in terms of form and contents. Some struggled with the poem and probably turned to page 246 of their editions where they found dates, details and a note on the use of “magnitude” which were then incorporated into answers. This, perhaps better than any other example on the paper, demonstrates a fairly widespread tendency to avoid close critical reading and substitute description and assertion. In the few minutes that candidates have to answer, a brief “map” such as the one suggested in the first sentence above would (with adequate support) be more than enough to guide a candidate towards high marks.
a720u10-jun17-04-ii: This question sparked a lot of interesting debate with some candidates rejecting the critical view out of hand, but others took a more nuanced view and saw in most of his writing a sense of awe inspired by the arts and literature of the past which was powerfully mingled with observations upon natural beauty as well as the rigours of the living world and the limitations imposed by mortality. There was some impressive coverage of the longer poems as well as the Odes but also some hints that all candidates at some centres were confident about only two or three poems and those were used irrespective of how relevant they were to the task.
a720u10-jun17-05-i: As with the Keats poem, the mood of this work is multi-layered – sombre, celebratory, doubtful, soberly reflective, anticipatory and, once again, if a short list such as this one had been used as a plan, many candidates could have avoided the fruitless syllable counting and often mistaken assertions about rhythm and rhyme patterns which, on their own, did little to reveal the ways Rossetti creates mood(s) in this poem.
a720u10-jun17-05-ii:
Many candidates interpreted “conventional morality” as religious duty and went no further; others wrote almost exclusively about Rossetti’s dedication to work with “fallen women” but in both cases the emphasis was often upon context and biography rather than the poetry. The best answers managed to range more widely on the subject of morality and made use of the contextual material above but through poems such as Goblin Market, No Thank You John and The Convent Threshold. Too many answers became bogged-down in biography and in the status of women which left little room for consideration of what is revealed by the poems themselves.
Summary and Advice:  Part (i) responses must stay focused upon the demands of AO1 and AO2; answers should be brief and there are examples of simple planning above which illustrate how a short, carefully constructed, relevant list would be quite sufficient to guide about 15 minutes of effective writing. Take careful account of the shaping element within the task – it is never an open opportunity to commentate on a poem or extract.  Advise candidates on the thinking underpinning the design of tasks; sequencing of questions and legitimate use of open books.  Look carefully at the balance of assessment objectives in Part (ii) and make sure that context is not overdone, or critical views pursued at the expense of AO1 and AO2.  Move attention away from poets’ biographies and more securely on to analyses of implicit meaning, technique and language.  Encourage the use of specialist terminology and the observation of structural features as part of an analysis of meaning and not as free-standing labels.
a720u10-jun17-06-q: Questions 6 and 7 Candidates seemed to prefer question 6 on disappointment over question 7 on the use of voices. As mentioned above, responses to question 6 were often unbalanced by over-long descriptions of the marital disappointments in the lives of both poets and lacked analysis of the ways in which the theme was presented. In many essays, reference to Hardy poems was very restricted - The Darkling Thrush and A Broken Appointment were very popular choices – both occur very early in the anthology – and these essays would have been improved with wider, more detailed reference. Others concentrated exclusively upon Poems of 1912-13 and these candidates tended to be most guilty of narrative treatments of Hardy’s marriage and bereavement. By contrast, there was wider-ranging reference to Eliot’s poetry with some very good writing on the The Waste Land and Preludes but also some very unconvincing attempts to link any expression of disappointment to his unsatisfactory first marriage. Many of those who attempted Question 7 showed a real appreciation of the different voices in Hardy, including that of an imagined ghost and the bitter-sweet or tragi-comic voices of The Ruined Maid. There was some very mature writing on Journey of The Magi, Gerontion and Portrait of a Lady as well as on The Waste Land

a720u10-jun17-08-q: Questions 8 and 9 These were not popular and only 3 responses to question 9 were seen. Those candidates showed some scope and variety in the materials they chose but it is not possible to provide a useful report on such tiny numbers.
a720u10-jun17-09-q: Questions 8 and 9 These were not popular and only 3 responses to question 9 were seen. Those candidates showed some scope and variety in the materials they chose but it is not possible to provide a useful report on such tiny numbers.
a720u10-jun17-10-q: Questions 10 and 11 This pairing was extremely popular and candidates preferred Question 11 and the opportunity to write about the presentation of pain rather than the details of domestic life in Question 10. The mean mark for 11 was a little higher than for 10 and candidates clearly found this question more accessible. Tedious as it may be, the point has to be made again that biographical narratives and assertions about the meanings of poems are not substitutes for critical analysis. No doubt some candidates will be disappointed with their marks as they gave copious accounts of “domestic details” and the “pain of experience” in relation to the poets’ marriage but said little or nothing about the poetic techniques used to communicate these matters. Essays drew upon a wide selection of Plath poems but were a little more restricted in references to Hughes: Full Moon and Little Frieda along with Bride and Groom Lie Hidden for Three Days were often used in response to question 10 while some of the Crow poems were used to address question 11. While it is understood that there are a lot of poems up to and including Rain on page 68, there was a strong sense that candidates had spent less time on their study of Hughes than on Plath.

a720u10-jun17-12-q: Questions 12 and 13 Another very popular pairing which produced some strong essays on the ways the poets observe the lives of others (question 12) and on the presentation of ideas about time in question 13. Candidates preferred Question 13 by a factor of 3 to 1 but the mean marks were identical. However, in both cases many ignored the critical view in the stem of the question (which should have helped to shape the response) and went on to write more generally about the observation of others’ lives or ideas about time. In many cases this meant that attention to AO5 was less relevant and effective as candidates attempted to use pre-learned critical quotations but ignored the idea of “little affection” in question 12 (which should have influenced the selection of poems) or the issue of fascination in question 13 which should have done the same. Consequently, essays were weakened under AO1 – for a lack of relevance; under AO2 for lack of purposefulness as well as under AO5 where the exploration of other readings was often not really relevant and was therefore little more than a description or acknowledgement of other readings. Once again, accounts of the poets’ lives and assertions about their relationships and sexuality figured largely and usually irrelevantly in many responses.

a720u10-jun17-14-q:
Questions 14 and 15 While there were comparatively few responses to this pairing, candidates certainly showed a marked preference for Question 14 on the presentation of beauty and brutality to 15 where they were asked about the presentation of ordinary experience. The mean marks were quite similar but just a little higher for the less popular choice. In their responses to Question 14, candidates found a good range of connections between the presentation of harsh realities in terms of political troubles and personal hardships as well as the combination of the brutal and the picturesque in the presentation of rural lives. In the responding to Question 15, candidates were sensitive to the transformative powers of not only the imagery and poetic language of both poets but also of the musical and rhythmic qualities achieved through their choices of form. Summary and Advice  Make sure that with all 5 assessment objectives in play, candidates understand how to achieve a sensible balance of attention and avoid over-emphasis upon AO3.  Make AO4 work purposeful and potentially illuminating by incorporating and developing ideas about connections with the process of close analysis so that AO2 and AO4 are closely bound.  Use biographical material with great care – be provisional rather than assertive and do not assume that all poems are written with a purpose connected to the actual events of a poet’s life.  In the two years available for the reading and study of both poets, try to be as wide- ranging as possible – there is some evidence that preparation has been very narrow in some cases.
The demands of this Component are fully understood by all examiners who would want me to pass on their messages of admiration and congratulations to those teachers and candidates who have worked so hard to produce some of the very highest quality responses.
9 EDUQAS
GCE A LEVEL ENGLISH LITERATURE
Summer 2017

a720u10-jun18-01-i: The best answers to this task took immediate note of the slant in the question which was to examine the ways in which Chaucer “shape[s] the reader’s response to Pluto in these lines.” The emphasis is squarely upon technique and picks up the point above about the specific nature of tasks in this section. Those who offered a general commentary on the lines could not show sound evidence of understanding or engaging with Chaucer’s techniques and therefore could not score highly under either of the AOs. There were still plenty of answers which relied upon general contextual comments on the treatment of women; or others which gave full accounts of the myth of Pluto and Proserpine and therefore did not earn very much credit.
a720u10-jun18-01-ii:
Most candidates managed to engage with the idea of a battle between the sexes but only the very best answers made full use of the terms in the question designed to trigger analytical discussion of context and possible readings of the poem. “Eternal” gives opportunities to range across relevant contexts and “surprising outcomes” provides a key to both medieval manners and values as well as suggesting a way of reading issues around
3 May’s success/failure or Proserpine’s defiance of her domineering husband. There were some authoritative and deeply impressive essays which wove together (with apt and economical textual support) the Merchant’s apparent defeat by his new wife; the implicit and explicit conflict between Januarie and May; the subversion of the courtly love tradition; the conflict between the supernaturals and, as a final seal on the essay, the Host’s nervous statements about his own marital problems. Lengthy, irrelevant or poorly deployed critical comments did not improve the quality of essays and there were still too many examples of writing where the majority of space was taken up with regurgitated contextual notes which acted as an impediment to creative engagement and critical analysis.
a720u10-jun18-02-i: Last year’s opening comment applies just as relevantly to this year’s responses: “Given that most candidates have had two years in which to study Donne, it was surprising to see so many bemused by this poem.” Some candidates who produced high quality essays on Donne in the next part had very little idea of the tone, attitudes or moods expressed in “Love’s Alchemy”. On the other hand, some very well-prepared candidates were able to analyse powerful feelings in subtle detail showing, with very economical support, where there might be outrage or mock rage; contempt; disappointment or distaste; where there might be irony or sincerity in the feelings expressed or where false feelings had been worked-up in support of a theoretical argument. To finish where this section of the report began, a quotation from last year's report: “Here as elsewhere in Part (i) responses there was a great deal of sterile feature spotting and “naming of parts”. Candidates must be convinced that there is no merit in the use of technical terminology simply for the purposes of labelling.”
a720u10-jun18-02-ii: Once again the point must be made that after two years' study of an Elizabethan poet it is perfectly reasonable to expect candidates to be familiar with the term “Renaissance” and with its implications of matters such as learning; manners; skills; discovery; travel and so on. This was the contextual trigger in the question and was offered as an opportunity for candidates to make use of what they had learned about the period and to encourage them away from assertions about Donne’s private life. The other part of the question “intellectual and emotional all-rounder” partly unpacks “Renaissance” while providing an opportunity for candidates to address critically a point of view. When this is fully understood, the need for carefully hoarded but often irrelevant or poorly focused contextual and critical material diminishes. There were some outstandingly good responses but as was the case last year it is time to emphasise to candidates that they should use with great care “John Carey’s and Simon Schama’s recent documentaries on the poet with all their playful speculation upon what John Donne might or might not have been doing/intending when he wrote his verse. Material such as the above, used as a primary study aid for Donne, has produced reams of unsupported assertion about the relationship between Donne’ s poems and his life which contribute nothing of value to a critical analysis of his poetry.” (Principal Examiner’s report 2017)
a720u10-jun18-03-i:
The key point here is once again the focus of the task. This is a conversation between the two characters so it is reasonable to ask how Milton shapes the reader’s response to both of them in the course of it. Carefully planned but appropriately brief responses showed through attention to key language points how a reader’s feelings might change over the course of these lines and very successful responses dealt in a sentence or so with the situation in the passage and examples such as the following stick in the mind and perfectly illustrate some of the skills required by this part of the paper: “Separated from her husband and protector by her own wilfulness, Eve’s naivety is exposed and exploited by the corrupting tempter.” Even
4 as the scene is set, the candidate wastes no opportunity to imply what our feelings might be towards the characters. Of course, after this introductory sentence the analysis becomes more explicitly focused on the techniques for shaping our feelings. Less successful responses described the circumstances in Eden at length or made detailed reference to what had brought about the separation of Adam and Eve. Please see notes below for further comment on writing skills.
a720u10-jun18-03-ii: As suggested above, the slant of Question 3 (i) should have focused candidates’ thinking about authority and the way it operates in Eden. The inclusion of the phrase “beyond the confines of Eden” encourages candidates to make use (with proper caution) of their contextual knowledge of both theological issues and the political circumstances of Milton’s world. Some well-informed and thoughtful essays carefully explored the idea of God the “absent friend” who remains outside the confines of Eden and, for subtle moral/theological reasons, is unwilling to assert his authority over Satan. Some also made fruitful reference to kingship and politics in Milton’s day which they saw reflected in his concerns over law making and breaking in Eden. In light of last year’s comments, “While many responses were of the highest quality, centres which choose Milton might do well to explore the theological and philosophical notions of sin and free will a little more thoroughly in order to avoid assertive and inaccurate approaches.”, there appeared to be some improvements in this area as many candidates addressed very complex issues with confidence. Those who allowed themselves lengthy, assertive descriptions of Milton’s domestic life were self- penalising.
a720u10-jun18-04-i: Famous for its rich ambiguity, this poem deserves the closest attention to the use of imagery and the creation of implicit meaning and mood. Many candidates were not prepared to go beyond a descriptive paraphrase or a limiting assertion of meaning when it would have been more appropriate in a task on the “use of imagery” to reveal layers of possible meaning and unresolved ambiguities rather than striving for certainties. I’m sure Keats would have approved of such an approach! Last year the point was made that in responses to Keats candidates often tried to “avoid close critical reading and substitute description and assertion.” Unfortunately this remains the case for some, but the best answers managed to say a great deal in a very short space pointing once again to the advantages enjoyed by those who have developed their writing skills and vocabulary as well as their experience of texts in their two years of study at A level.
a720u10-jun18-04-ii: The wording of this question allowed candidates to make use of what they had learned about the literary and cultural context of the Romantic period and the notion of “rebellion” allowed them to consider readings of the poetry which provide different views of reality from those supported by the rationalism of the Enlightenment. There are, of course, other ways of seeing Keats as a soul in rebellion and some made very strong cases for the ways in which Keats challenges the restrictions imposed by mortality/illness or those placed upon conventional human relationships. There was some very thoughtful work on this topic and it is a real pleasure to see how much some candidates have enjoyed their study of Keats. As always though, less satisfactory responses regurgitated “data” about Keats’ personal life and career without establishing clear and relevant relationships between that and the poetry.
a720u10-jun18-05-i:
The direction to examine poetic techniques is one of the group of “command lines” used in this section to illicit a literary-critical response. The necessary brevity of the response calls for careful planning and preparation in all cases but particularly so where there are
5 potentially so many angles to take: imagery; symbolism; language choices; tone; structure; implicit meaning and so on. Candidates need to use good judgement here and understand that only a selection of material can possibly be covered in the time allotted. This calls for a brave use of time at the start of the process where a few minutes spent re-reading and planning a coherent selection of relevant points will pay real dividends. The issue of time- management is mentioned over and over again by examiners and centres are advised that this should be an integral part of candidates’ preparation.
a720u10-jun18-05-ii:
Responses to Q5 (i) should have loosened-up candidates’ thinking about the operation of the creative imagination and the ways in which ideas and attitudes are liberated by it. However, work on Q5 (i) will also have reminded candidates that however creative and inventive the writer might be there are potential cultural restrictions which have to be negotiated. This is not material for the first part of the response but candidates now had a full opportunity to make use of their contextual ideas as they addressed “restrictions of life as a Victorian woman” and judged to what extent Rossetti is freed from such restrictions by her art. It was pleasing to see how widely candidates ranged and how closely they engaged with Rossetti’s work in the context of a rule-based society as she considered amongst other things issues around religious devotion; femininity; patriarchal attitudes and romantic relationships. However, once again to quote from last year’s report: “Too many answers became bogged-down in biography and in the status of women which left little room for consideration of what is revealed by the poems themselves.”
Key Points:
 Part (i) responses must stay focused upon the demands of AO1 and AO2; answers should be brief and there should be evidence of basic planning which would be sufficient to guide about 15 minutes of effective writing. Take careful account of the shaping element within the task – it is never an open opportunity to commentate on a poem or extract.  Centres should advise candidates on the thinking underpinning the design of tasks; sequencing of questions and legitimate use of open books.  Look carefully at the balance of assessment objectives in Part (ii) and make sure that context is not overdone, or critical views pursued at the expense of AO1 and AO2.  Move attention away from poets’ biographies and more securely on to analyses of features such as implicit meaning, technique and language.  Encourage the use of specialist terminology and the observation of structural features as part of an analysis of meaning and not as free-standing labels.  Candidates should avoid a technique which boils down to “assert relevance of poem to task – work through poem offering general commentary and asserting meaning – re-assert relevance.” Those whose writing was otherwise fluent and accurate failed to make an impression with this non-analytical, poorly supported approach.  Taking the example from a candidate’s writing on Milton above, use this as a starting point for developing flexible strategies for improving the quality and confidence of candidates’ written expression.
a720u10-jun18-06-q:
I believe it is worth offering an edited version of last year’s overview of this section: Just like Section A, this is an open book examination and it relieves candidates of the effort of memorising large amounts of verse. Instead, the demands are upon writing a substantial essay which requires balanced attention to all the assessment objectives which apply to English Literature.
The word “balanced” above is crucial because candidates need to be clearly aware that 20 marks are earned through attention to AO2 and “the ways in which meanings are shaped”. The other 4 assessment objectives are evenly weighted at 10 marks each. The point is made starkly because there was so much evidence of candidates writing extensively about what they considered to be relevant contexts but, as in Section A, these approaches often went no further than descriptions of poets’ private lives.
In addition to considering contexts and other readings; showing creative engagement and critical analysis, candidates are required to “explore connections across literary texts” in their responses to a total of at least 4 poems – 2 by each writer in the pair. The evidence suggests that this element (AO4) has not been well understood by significant numbers of candidates.
By far the best way of addressing AO4 is to make connections throughout the analysis of paired poems so that AO2 and AO4 seem almost inseparable as they become functions of each other.
Lastly, candidates need to think very carefully about their timings in this section. Many, it seemed, had used every minute of the hour to write sprawling responses which were not always relevant and which attempted to name check as many poems as possible. It would be much better to spend a sensible amount of time deconstructing the question; choosing and re-reading a selection of at least 4 poems in order to re-focus ideas and then writing a simple plan before embarking on the final product. As a general rule, shorter, better-focused essays with brief but apt textual support will achieve the higher bands.
By far the most popular pairing in this section was Larkin and Duffy. The second most popular choice was Hughes and Plath, followed by Eliot and Hardy, Heaney and Sheers. Very few candidates responded to the questions on Lawrence and Clarke.
a720u10-jun18-07-q:
Question 7 on the voices and portraits being those of characters “adrift in an uncaring world” proved the more popular choice and produced some excellent responses with genuine insight into the ways in which the poets had created sombre; pained or neurotic voices operating in hostile worlds. There were some thoughtful and clever connections between the ways in which the poets presented alienation and the best essays rose above the personal/biographical and looked at alienation as a wider cultural issue. It was a little alarming (presumably after two years’ study in most cases) to see how few candidates ventured outside Hardy’s poems of 1912-13. The temptation for some to write at length about Emma Hardy’s estrangement from her husband and link this to Eliot’s own marital problems proved too much and tended to produce assertive, low-scoring essays with insufficient attention to the heavily weighted AO2. As has been said so often, biographical material in measured doses can be a valid and effective way of addressing context provided it is linked through analysis rather than assertion to relevant text.
There was a little less enthusiasm for Hardy’s and Eliot’s use of weather and seasons in Question 6 but still there were some strong answers where candidates had made sensible use of the critical quotation and explored how such imagery might be the “key to meaning”
7 as well as a factor in creating mood and atmosphere. There are some very obvious poems from both poets which were sensible choices for close study but once again, there does appear to be a fairly restricted programme at some centres where all candidates used the same 4 poems and in some cases these were not the best to support writing on this topic. “The Ruined Maid” is popular for very good reasons but can only be seen as tangential when writing a relevant response to this task.
a720u10-jun18-08-q: As was the case last year, the responses to this pairing were small and it is not possible to offer general conclusions about candidates’ approaches. Those who did respond showed a preference for Q9 on the poets’ use of “older, primitive worlds” and there were some sensible analyses of the ways in which the natural world, human significance and human society were viewed through the lens of an imagined distant past as well as through the consideration of older or primitive life forms.

a720u10-jun18-10-q: As was the case in 2017, this pairing was extremely popular with candidates showing a slight preference for Q10 on “death and decay” over Q11 which asked candidates to consider the potential offensiveness of poetry in a culture which promoted “directness and honesty in the arts.” In their responses to both questions candidates readily lapsed into context-driven accounts of suicide; illness; dysfunctional personal relationships; childhoods brutalised by bereavement or the realities of the natural word in Yorkshire and so on. In some ways this is understandable but in terms of relevance and intellectual challenge these are the “low-hanging fruit” and in many cases produced descriptive, assertive writing which was divorced from textual analysis. For those many centres which will continue to study Plath and Hughes, there is a clear need to re-focus attention on the literary qualities of the poems and how they might be mutually illuminating. Advice in this report and elsewhere talks of the need to establish connections between poems and poets on the basis of the poetry itself rather than upon assertions such as, “these poems are closely connected because Ted and Sylvia were both experiencing conflict in their marriage just weeks before Sylvia’s suicide.” Candidates must be shown that this chatty approach is typical of low-end feature journalism rather than literary analysis. It is worth repeating that AO2 and AO4 connect seamlessly in high quality literary analysis.

a720u10-jun18-12-q: Larkin and Duffy continue to interest a very large number of candidates but, as with Hughes and Plath above, there is a narrowing tendency to see the poems as pure, factual autobiography rather than artistic creations. This causes essays to swerve away at the earliest possible stage from considerations of the ways meaning is made with regard to the poets’ approach to popular culture or in Q13 the presentation of unhappiness. The most successful essays had obviously spent time at the planning stage for Q12 deciding what might be meant by popular culture and how far the definition would stretch. Confident candidates were able to analyse the presentation of “cut-price” weddings; consumerism; leisure pursuits and sentimental love songs alongside the presentation of pop music; quiz shows; fashion and sensational media. The best answers to Q13 were equally careful in observing different kinds or degrees of unhappiness – lack of fulfilment; rejection; isolation; disappointment; self-loathing and regret instead of offering generalised assertions about misery or pain inevitably linked to the “facts” of the poets 'lives. Once again, centres are advised to re-focus candidates' attention away from the careers or personal habits of both poets and squarely onto the ways the poems are made and how they might connect in illuminating ways. The conclusion to last year’s comments on this pairing was as follows, “accounts of the poets’ lives and assertions about their relationships and sexuality figured largely and usually irrelevantly in many responses.” Getting the balance right and viewing contextual material through the poems themselves is central to successful writing.

a720u10-jun18-14-q:
Once again this year there were, comparatively, very few responses to this pairing, and barely enough to arrive at any general conclusions. There was a handful of responses to Q14 and “the importance of the past” where candidates made sensible references to Irish history but some were led astray by what they had learned about Sheers as a novelist and screen writer and tended to make references to his work on the first and second world wars. However, there was effective writing on family circumstances and locations as factors in shaping poetic sensibilities. The very few responses seen to Q15 were skewed quite markedly towards politics and terrorism in Heaney’s case but this produced challenges when making connections with Sheers. There are other very obvious elements in the poems such as colourful/typical characters and folk culture which would have made points of connection and allowed for a full exploration of comparisons as well as contrasts. As with all of the poets above, care must be taken when dealing with the poets’ biographies – candidates must be encouraged to see the ways life experiences have been made into art rather than regarding poems as simple records of experience.
Key Points:
 Make sure that, with all 5 assessment objectives in play, candidates understand how to achieve a sensible balance of attention and avoid over-emphasis upon AO3.  Make AO4 work purposeful and potentially illuminating by incorporating and developing ideas about connections with the process of close analysis so that AO2 and AO4 are closely bound.  Use biographical material with great care – be provisional rather than assertive and do not assume that all poems are written with a purpose connected to the actual events of a poet’s life.  In the two years available for the reading and study of both poets, try to be as wide- ranging as possible – there is some evidence that preparation has been very narrow in some cases.  There is sufficient time in Section B to allow for careful choosing of material and planning an effective response: candidates must be persuaded that shorter, better focused, analytical writing will always do better than badly organised, lengthy descriptive/assertive accounts.  Encourage mature, effective writing strategies - from the use of topic sentences to developing general vocabulary and varied sentence structures to achieve economy and show more secure creative engagement.
The demands of this component are fully understood by all examiners who would want me to pass on their messages of admiration and congratulation to those teachers and candidates who have worked so hard to produce some of the very highest quality responses.

a720u10-jun19-01-i:
Part (i) responses to Chaucer were sometimes off target as candidates who had prepared to write about the Januarie/May relationship were determined to do so and consequently missed all of the rich imagery relating to Damian which is present throughout the passage but especially towards the end. Close focus on the selected lines and the designated task is of paramount importance.
In planning their responses to part (ii) candidates should have taken careful note of the AO3 and AO5 triggers in the question which are expanded here as an example of the best approach to this and other questions of the pre-1900 poetry collections. “Beneath the surface of this entertaining and bawdy tale we find a serious examination of obligation and loyalty.” Explore this view.” Apart from the obvious invitation to consider implicit meaning “beneath the surface” (AO2), for AO3, candidates should have seen an opportunity to draw upon what they knew about medieval entertainment – court life; oral tradition; moral values then and now . “Bawdy tale” leads into French, Italian and classical literary models. “Obligation and Loyalty” refers to medieval values of service and master/servant relationships and marriage customs. From here, essays could have branched out into courtly love and the distortion or possible parodying of this tradition as part of the robust entertainment on offer to Chaucer’s audience, and how ideas about any or all of these matters might be seen differently by a modern audience. To have identified and isolated these issues and then approached them selectively via the text itself would have provided a relevant framework for addressing AO3.
Similarly with AO5, careful reading of the question should reveal where there are different possible readings of the material. For instance, some might argue that there is no “serious examination” which some readers have claimed but the driving force of the Prologue and Tale is consistently comical and satirical. Others might see the Prologue and Tale as primarily didactic rather than simply entertaining and so on. Close consideration of the view that is offered in the question will always be preferable to imported, irrelevant material.

a720u10-jun19-02-i:
Part (i) answers to Donne were often marred by a systematic, line by line explanation of what the poem “means”. Descriptive or narrative responses fill pages but, however fluent and accurately written they may be, they are unable to move above Band 2 unless there is an attempt at relevant analysis rather than descriptive commentary. In this case, a few minutes planning and selection of the key images would have paid dividends. Many candidates could not restrain themselves from talking about Donne’s “sinful” youth (often with colourful asserted detail) and his abandonment of his Roman Catholic faith. AO3 is not rewarded here.
In the second part of the question relevant AO3 material was clearly signposted in the idea of “passionate feelings, whether sacred or profane.” This wording opens up opportunities to consider C16/17th attitudes towards romance and courtship; the Petrarchan tradition; moral values then and now and so on. The wording allows these to be held-up against religious belief and conventions of worship which applied in Donne’s time.
For AO5, candidates have the opportunity to argue that some readers might consider that intellectual rigour is the actual driving force of Donne’s poetry and that passion of whatever sort is secondary.
Chaucer and Donne are by far the most popular choices on this paper and so the examples above, which can be adapted to apply to any of the poets below, have been developed at some length. It is hoped that these examples might prompt practice exercises in the classroom on any of the poets, so that candidates can be better trained to read tasks attentively and plan their responses appropriately, rather than embarking too quickly upon over-long, repetitive “hit or miss” responses.

a720u10-jun19-03-i:
Most candidates realised that in this extract there is a serious falling-out between Adam and Eve but it was the ways in which Milton presented their aggressive strategies which required analysis. Many candidates spent far too long contextualising the episode and too little time on the techniques employed.
In part (ii), candidates should have registered the AO2 triggers in “dramatized and humanised” – understood that the issues under consideration in Book IX constitute some of the most common themes in abstract sermons but here Milton’s art brings both entertainment and immediate relevance to his readers of whatever period i.e. “Timeless”. “Revolt and disobedience” open up a range of AO3 approaches with the opportunities to consider the relevance and applicability of the comment as a starter for AO5.

a720u10-jun19-04-i:
Part (i) here is a very good example of the specific directions in questions of this sort. The extract was chosen for the rich sensuousness of the imagery and candidates were asked to consider the ways in which Keats engages the reader’s senses. This is asking for responses to focus on the pure pleasure of reading and over- contextualising or seeking obscure symbolic significance was a distraction from the designated task.
In part (ii), candidates should have been careful and selective in the ways in which they addressed the age of “intellectual enlightenment” – some grasped an opportunity to write extensively about science and medicine (linking to Keats’ occupation) without sufficient reference to the texts to allow them to balance the appeal to readers’ emotions rather than their interest in ideas – moral, philosophical, theological and so on. Some responded thoughtfully and made good use of Keats’ interests in time, mortality, antiquity and literature to challenge the premise of the task.

a720u10-jun19-05-i:
This is possibly one of the best poems to demonstrate the mercurial twists and turns which Rossetti often brings about over a very short space. Careful planning was essential here – candidates needed to have identified the “range” of emotions and how one shifted into another before they started to write. Without planning, many responses simply worked through line by line trying to identify different emotions – this is descriptive commentary and quite different from the analysis of technique.
In part (ii), the AO3 triggers are clear in the mention of Christianity but also in the great age of sermons candidates might have been expected to understand how Rossetti takes her place amongst persuasive religious writers but approaches moral teaching in a different and distinctive way. From an AO5 point of view, “primary intention” might have been challenged with the widely held belief that so much of Rossetti’s writing is more prayer than instruction so some readers would not be inclined to apply wholesale the assertion in the task.

a720u10-jun19-06-q:
Question 6 proved to be the more popular choice and the best answers were extremely well-informed about both poets’ knowledge and understanding of the both the recent and distant past whether this was applied to the history of families and relationships or the much larger issues of religion, mythology and human conflict. 'The Waste Land' and poems such as 'The Darkling Thrush' provided useful connections. Weaker answers tended to assert points about the personal histories of both writers or to reproduce badly digested notes on Victorian culture and Modernism.
There were very few responses to Question 7 but those that were seen had some mature and well-informed ideas about religion and the supernatural. The best responses to Hardy moved beyond the very popular poems of 1912–13 and obvious choices such as ‘The Haunter’ and “The Voice” and were able to demonstrate an understanding of the ways in which the imagination gives new life to departed people and past times. Good connections were made between this and Eliot’s ability to present religious miracle and other supernatural experience in poems such as “Journey of The Magi” or “The Hollow Men” in terms of common human experience.
a720u10-jun19-10-q:
This is the second most popular pairing on the paper and there is a very broad range of quality in the responses. The task in Question 10 invited an analysis of the presentation of “personal experience” by the two poets and those who built their responses around contrasts between the deeply personal, confessional style of Plath and the more objective, implicit presentation of personal experience/feeling in most of Hughes’ poems were very successful. Those who told detailed tales of Plath’s suicide and Hughes’ infidelities left themselves little or no time to analyse the poems or to make valid connections.
There were very strong responses to Question 11 too but “disturbing” was taken too much for granted and many candidates did not attempt to anatomise what might be meant by a reader’s disturbance – moral? aesthetic? intellectual? discussion of this element of the question might have helped to keep responses on track, open up a wider range of poetry and avoid the pitfall of an over-emphasis upon biographical gossip.
a720u10-jun19-12-q:
Larkin and Duffy are by far the most popular pairing on this paper. But, as mentioned above, many responses are marred by an over-emphasis upon biographical detail which is asserted and often misapplied. Examples are too numerous to detail, but there is an urgent case here for candidates to be persuaded not to indulge in extensive writing about the lives of poets and attempt to draw equivalences between issues such as sexuality and marital status and the voices presented in the poems. There may be such equivalences but these need to be considered tentatively and while 'A Study of Reading Habits' might be an autobiographical poem it is very much more than that and candidates must resist the urge to reduce and simplify great art into a cipher for a poet’s actual experience. Those who concentrated exclusively in their responses to Question 12 upon the changes in the historical lives of Larkin and Duffy missed the point and largely failed to consider the ways in which “Larkin and Duffy present ideas about change.” which requires a much more conceptual and analytical approach than is possible when asserting biographical “facts”.
There were some very strong responses to Question 13, the presentation of human relationships, and it was pleasing to see candidates offering a broad range of material covering family, romance, professional relationships and more abstract ideas about relationships between people and places and how one reflects the other.
a720u10-jun19-14-q:
Very few centres choose this pairing but those that did produced some strong answers on human relationships and the “presentation of human intimacy” (Question 14). It was pleasing to read some mature responses which did not interpret intimacy only in terms of sexual relationships but also in terms of the intimacies enjoyed by relationships across the generations or between friends and family. There was some very well informed and sensitive writing on these issues.
While Question 15 seemed to generate more direct writing about the actual life experiences of the poets rather than the more abstract idea of how other people and their achievements seem to inspire writing and how this is presented, there were still some strong and well-informed responses. Approaches showed how the values, ambitions and sentiments expressed in the work of both poets might have been inspired by as broad a range of characters as other famous writers; family members; apparently unremarkable people in bars or reckless drivers.
Summary of key points
• In Section A part (i) questions candidates must be mindful of the focus of the task and take time to plan accordingly. • In Section A part (ii) questions take careful note of the AO3 and AO5 triggers and make these the starting point for planning and selecting appropriate material. • In Section B responses avoid the temptation to assert biographical detail which has little or no bearing upon the task and which obscures rather than enhances literary-critical approaches. • Make connections between poets on the basis of their writing rather than the details of their lives. • By all means make use of the terminology associated with English Literature in order to support an academic register of writing, but avoid simple labelling, the identification of word classes or grammatical constructions simply to display knowledge. • Make sure that your handwriting can be read.

a720u10-jun22-01-i:
1(i) is not an invitation to describe Januarie: responses needed to take full account of Chaucer’s techniques in shaping readers’ responses and to say what those responses are likely to be. Many responses were heavy-handed in asserting equivalences between January and the animals mentioned in the passage. There seemed to be a lot of misunderstanding (not helped by hints in the text notes) about the significance of Pyk and Pikerel with many suggesting the primary function of the references is to cast Januarie as a predatory Pyk and May as the smaller, younger pikerel. Very few seemed to realise that these references relate to appetite in the same way that old boef and tender veel refer to gastronomic preferences (pike were fish for the table in Chaucer’s day) with overtones perhaps of predatory sexual desire. Candidates must try to differentiate between allusions (which might put us in mind of something) and metaphors or similes which make direct reference.
1(ii) was generally well-handled but some were distracted by a debate about whose selfishness deserved most punishment followed by lengthy accounts of feminist readings which might regard May as fully justified in her deceit of January and properly rewarded with her escape at the end of the Tale. This does not, of course, do justice to the ambiguity of Chaucer’s conclusion. There were some odd ideas about Chaucer writing for a medieval feminist audience which could not be supported. Care should be taken in distinguishing between the contexts in which texts are written and those in which they are received.

For 2(i), candidates were not asked to describe the mood and atmosphere but to explore Donne’s poetic techniques. Better answers did not work through the stanzas offering general commentary but identified the power of image patterns and the effects of structure and cadence.

a720u10-jun22-03-i:
In 3(i) weaker responses simply described Satan’s appearance and behaviour. Stronger responses saw that there were several elements to the presentation of temptation involving flattery; stimulation of appetite; deceitful exampling of Satan’s own fictious success and subtle appeals to Eve’s latent ambition.
For 3(ii) there was some awkwardness in many responses where ‘deceit’ was confused with ‘disobedience’ giving rise to self-contradictory ideas about deceiving the omniscient God. The limitations of candidates’ own vocabulary became apparent with many examples of ‘deceiting’ and the ubiquitous use of ‘want’ instead of desire, need, covet and so on. Very few probed ideas of self-deceit or the seeds of deceit implicit in Adam’s and Eve’s earliest exchanges which was disappointing. Many wanted to show off all they had learned about the epic and rhetoric without much regard to relevance. Milton’s treatment of his daughters and muddled ideas about his theological, social and political beliefs were, once again, often mentioned without regard to relevance.

Many wanted to show off all they had learned about the epic and rhetoric without much regard to relevance. Milton’s treatment of his daughters and muddled ideas about his theological, social and political beliefs were, once again, often mentioned without regard to relevance.

For 4(i) there were further issues of descriptive writing rather than exploration of technique with regard to word choice, structure and tone.

Once again, it is a matter of reading subtext and engaging with poetic techniques rather than describing.

Confident responses pointed to satirical flavours and wry humour in both poets’ work.

For Question 13, there were some strong responses with interesting interpretations of what might be signalled by ‘uncivilised’ and ‘instinctive’. Biographical references abounded (e.g., Plath’s pregnancy and Hughes’ shamanism) which, as in other pairings, sometimes overwhelmed critical analysis of the poetry.
Some excellent debates were seen in essays on Question 14 and, as hoped, the better essays came up with “Yes…but” responses which cleverly explored the half -truth stated in the task. It was a slightly different question format from previous years which seemed to work well in opening up opportunities. As is so often the case, the major drawback was asserted and often inaccurate biographical material which was allowed to stand for itself and was not successfully connected with the poets’ ideas and techniques.

a720u10-jun22-15-q: Question 15 was a popular choice and there were plenty of competent responses. Some were confident enough to explore the nuances of different sorts of relationship such as parent / child as well as the more obvious romantic dimension. Dislocated writing about the poets’ real lives continues to be a problem – obviously tempting with this particular task – but candidates need to be more aware of literary concepts and to avoid creating literal equivalences between poems and the ‘facts’ of the poets’ lives. There were lengthy and sweeping accounts of Larkin’s relationships and some extreme cases of using a poem such as ‘Havisham’ merely as brief introductions to long accounts of how Duffy herself had suffered hurt and betrayal.
a720u10-jun22-16-q: Question 16 was also popular and there were some quite subtle and wide-ranging treatments of ‘disillusionment’ in better essays. Weaker responses tended to give accounts of how relationships had failed (i.e. mostly focused on ‘Talking in Bed’ or ‘Adultery’) leaving the personae disappointed or disillusioned rather than upon more nuanced presentations of different sorts of disillusionment.
a720u10-jun22-17-q:
It was gratifying to see more interest in this pairing from centres outside Ireland and Wales. Unfortunately, some responses to Question 17 chose to concentrate on ‘emotions’ rather than ‘senses’ which caused a loss of direct focus but, in most cases, they were still able to make valid and supported points.
It was a great pleasure to read a number of thoughtful and clearly inspired responses to Question 18. Those who chose it had little trouble in interpreting ‘sublime’ and offered some very interesting approaches taking in the transformation of the visual world through the poets’ imagery and cadences, as well as the elevation of what might be taken for ordinary or simple human feelings and behaviour which were shown to be especially dignified or of central cultural importance and, by extension, sublime.
Summary of key points
 Teachers responsible for delivering English Language, English Language and Literature and English Literature at A level should be sure that language used in the different classrooms and in practice written work meets the specific demands of the subject. The discussion of poetry in the English Literature classroom should concentrate upon vocabulary choices; implicit meaning; tone; auditory effects; imagery and literary devices such as metaphor, simile, hyperbole and so on. Most importantly, when making use of the technical terms from the literature “toolbox”, candidates must make sure they are not simply feature-spotting but analysing how such features function in making meaning.
 Specific work needs to be done in many cases upon the development of range and precision in candidates active vocabularies. In the past, teachers have devised vocabulary-based word games at the introductory stage of lessons where the focus and content of the lesson is anticipated. This hardly needs explaining, but if a poem of a certain sort will be the focus of the lesson, then students might be invited as a starter to develop as much vocabulary as possible out of the key word ‘sad’ - leading them perhaps to ‘miserable’; ‘gloomy’; ‘wretched’; ‘desolate’; ‘dejected’ and so on. Discussions about nuanced differences and the emotional ‘temperature’ of words will be greatly beneficial. The important thing is to raise awareness of the importance of demonstrating clear engagement when writing about poetry through effective word choices.
5  There are useful materials available on the WJEC and Eduqas website which will help students to see the differences between descriptive writing, commentary and analysis. A failure to write analytically is the primary reason for depressed marks in this subject.
 Take care that well-intended support for students does not produce an over-rigid approach to the examination so that candidates are unprepared to interpret the specific demands of questions and respond freshly and relevantly.
 Candidates should be dissuaded from attempting to include every fragment of critical comment they have learned in the course of study. Exercises designed to help students apply what they know about other interpretations relevantly, and to provide examples of the development of critical discussions would be of great benefit.
 The same applies to contextual knowledge. The key is to be found in whether or not a contextual reference can be connected to the ways in which the poet makes meaning. In other words, AO2 and AO3 should be seen as bonded elements. Assertion should be discouraged and the presentation of simple equivalences between poetry and the real lives of writers. “…this is about a time when x did y” should be treated with caution.
 Some damaging tendencies, which have been gradually increasing over recent years in both the delivery of the specification and in candidates’ responses to tasks, have now become severe and quite widespread; they are summarised in the table below.
Issue Comments  Sterile labelling of features using terms from the English Language / linguistics toolbox.
One examiner describes the use of terminology from linguistics in literary essays as “attempting to assemble Lego with a Meccano toolbox”. Another describes simple identification of features such as asyndetic lists, noun phrases or semantic fields as “weighing and measuring”. Once a feature such as these has been identified and labelled in a literary essay there is really not much more to say about it; it very rarely contributes to literary analysis but it leaves the candidate with the mistaken impression that they have written something valuable which should earn credit under either AO1 or AO2. Any use of technical terminology must have a direct and relevant role in analysing the ways in which meaning is made.  Even taking account of the reduced content which applied this year, the further narrowing of textual study created problems for candidates.
It was sometimes alarming to see in both Section A and Section B that candidates from the same centre had only the same 3 or 4 poems with which to support their responses. This is related to the point about ‘template essays’ below and candidates often resorted to a ‘hit-and-hope’ approach with unsatisfactory attempts to make memorised notes on the poems fit the set tasks. A much more flexible and wide-ranging approach to the study of poetry is strongly recommended.
6  Lack of development and range in candidates’ own vocabulary which seriously limits their ability to express themselves clearly and effectively. This often prevents candidates from achieving an appropriate tone or register in their essays.
AO1 requires candidates to aim for clarity, engagement and an academic register. Centres are strongly advised to give adequate time and attention to the development of personal vocabulary through whatever means seems appropriate. Thesaurus word games which are geared towards the material to follow as a warm- up in the classroom might work for many. …

a720u10-jun23-01-i: A large number of responses took a descriptive approach to the extract and placed the emphasis on Januarie himself whereas the task asks candidates to analyse the ways in which Chaucer suggests the Merchant’s attitudes as he begins his tale about the old knight. Some seemed to come to an understanding of the task in the last sentence or two where points about the Merchant’s bitterness were made but these were dislocated from the rest of the response. This provides good evidence for the necessity of careful consideration and planning even for these brief responses.
a720u10-jun23-01-ii: Candidates were mostly very comfortable with how Chaucer ‘points the finger critically’ but many were less successful at engaging with the idea of humour. The best answers were very assured about what might be considered humorous in a C14th context; what might be appreciated by a modern reader and what elements of humour could be shared across the ages.
a720u10-jun23-02-i: The mention of ‘garden’, ‘serpent’ and ‘transubstantiates’ presented many candidates with the temptation to write extensively about biblical and religious contexts. This is perhaps an excellent opportunity for us to note the difference between a nod to context which supports analysis and an extended display of contextual knowledge which interrupts analysis. If a candidate writes, “Donne’s claim that he has brought within him the ‘serpent’ that contaminates the beauty of the garden has inescapable associations with the fall of man which contributes to the poem’s mood of doom and misery”, then the emphasis remains upon the ways in which Donne makes meaning (AO2). If, on the other hand, a candidate writes, “Donne mentions a serpent which reminds us of the events in the Book of Genesis where Eve is working alone and is confronted by Satan disguised as a serpent who then…”, this becomes an extended display of contextual knowledge (AO3) which is not rewarded in part (i) responses.
a720u10-jun23-02-ii: This question was very well handled by many candidates who offered a very sensible balance of attention to both sacred and secular poems showing intelligent engagement with the different sorts of passion involved; the ways in which Donne had deliberately confused them and how frustrations appeared to be both serious and exaggerated for comic or satirical purposes. Those who put all the emphasis upon Donne’s passion for his wife and the story of their relationship or upon other biographical elements such as Donne’s religious affiliations, largely missed the opportunity to analyse the poetry in the light of the view in the question and, consequently, penalised themselves.
a720u10-jun23-03-i: Descriptions of Adam’s and Eve’s behaviour here without analysing how their words, actions and Milton’s imagery worked together to create a mood of sensuality missed the point of the question. The task demands an examination of technique and here is a good opportunity to emphasise point made in the overview of this component above which reminds candidates that they will never be asked to describe an extract or poem.
a720u10-jun23-03-ii: There were some very ambitious responses to this task, some of which took issue with the question and argued persuasively that far from being reduced to a recognizable human, Adam in particular was presented as a fallen heroic figure of myth and legend. Most took a very sensible overview of the development of Adam and Eve towards demonstrating clearly recognisable human weakness, showing how language choices, tone of speeches and imagery brought about this development and a change in readers’ responses.
a720u10-jun23-04-i: Many who responded to this question seemed uncomfortable with the poem ‘A Poison Tree’ and a significant number of candidates had little idea of how the imagery worked in structuring an extended metaphor or allegory. Some tried to impose meaning by writing extensively about friendship; others felt the poem might celebrate nature and there was some confusion about who lay outstretched beneath the tree at the conclusion. This might be evidence of highly selective study, as outlined in the overview at the beginning of this report.
a720u10-jun23-04-ii: Once again with reference to the comment grid from the overview above, this was not an invitation to describe or ‘work through’ some of Blake’s poems which feature aspects of nature. Those who took this approach were not able to progress beyond Band 2 but responses which focused on Blake’s presentation of the natural world and what it reveals about the poet’s ‘view of life’ were more successful. Some strayed too far from the brief and wrote a fairly standard essay on Blake’s social conscience with little or no attention to the ways in which the presentation of the natural world provides relevant insight.
a720u10-jun23-05-i: It is understood that candidates have a number of poems to study, but ‘Sweet Death’ comes early in the collection and it is one which focuses so many of the poet’s beliefs and attitudes that it should be well known. For some candidates, however, it seemed to be an unseen text. They struggled to move beyond a description of what the poem seems to be about rather than attempt an analysis of the ways in which the image patterns work to present a set of ideas about mortal life and the afterlife, culminating in a prayer-like final stanza brining all thoughts and feelings together in the image of ‘harvest’. Candidates had been asked about the use of imagery’ but too many became bogged-down in rhyme patterns, syllable counts and the sterile application of technical terms with which to measure the verse. Attention is drawn to the comment table in the overview above and to the introduction to Section A: It is vital that candidates pay attention to the specific demands of Part (i) tasks.
a720u10-jun23-05-ii: ‘Sweet Death’ should have provided an ideal launchpad for this essay and it is perfectly legitimate for part (ii) essays to make brief reference to the chosen poem in part (i), provided this does not consist of much more than introductory remarks. In order to achieve high bands under all four AOs which apply here, candidate need to show some range in their selection of material so as to give themselves opportunities of showing their skill at structuring a relevant response and analysing soundly while making purposeful and sound use of contexts and other readings. Many responses focused exclusively upon Rossetti’s ideas of sin and damnation / redemption to illustrate her spiritual perspective – a perfectly legitimate approach – and made good use of poems such as ‘An Apple Gathering’, ‘Goblin Market’ or ‘A Daughter of Eve’ but weaker responses tended to spend too much time describing biographical detail (such as Rossetti’s work with ‘fallen women’) rather than keeping the focus upon analysis of the poems.
a720u10-jun23-06-q: There were some very strong responses to this question with close and detailed analysis of imagery in both poets’ work. Imaginative and thoughtful connections were made in terms of mood, atmosphere and attitudes as many candidates appreciated how both poets made use of the senses to connect abstract thoughts with details of the physical world. Most appreciated the emotional intensity of recollecting the precise clothing of a departed lover or the horror /disgust implicit in the observation of “smoke that rubs its muzzle on the window-panes”. Most candidates were very well- informed and chose material for analysis from an impressive range of sources.
a720u10-jun23-07-q: This was a more popular option than Question 6 and while it was quite well handled in many cases it did not produce as many essays with a convincing literary focus. The best essays managed to consider change from a broad perspective taking in cultural / historical changes (there was some impressive writing on ‘The Wasteland’) as well as considering change at a personal level. However, weaker responses moved directly to biographical details, mostly Hardy’s bereavement, Eliot’s relationships and his conversion to Anglicanism. Please see the comment table in the overview above regarding the effective and judicious use of contextual details, especially biographies of modern poets. It is a vital skill and candidates must keep their work on contexts closely connected to analysis.
