a720u10-jun23-10-q: Although not quite as popular a choice as Question 11, this task produced some excellent writing and some thoughtfully chosen poems which allowed a detailed exploration of the ways in which the poets perceived and presented hostility and comfortlessness in nature. If anything, candidates could have worked a little more at making productive comparisons (AO4) and developing ideas about comparisons and contrasts between the language, imagery and forms employed by both poets. As they prepare for Section B, candidates should have plenty of opportunities to analyse poems by the different poets side-by-side and achieve a clear understanding of how the double-weighted AO2 can be addressed through analytical rather than descriptive efforts to make connections (AO4).
a720u10-jun23-11-q: When we ask about the poets themselves being the focus of their work, it is less biographical details that we are seeking (although they come into it) and more evidence of the poets’ self-analysis or self-discovery through their poetry. This pairing seems to attract more simple, biographical accounts than other options on Component 1. Centres are strongly advised to guide candidates beyond the colourful details of the poets’ lives and explore the significance and influence of wider cultural and social contexts which can be shown to have influenced their work, and the ways in which it is read and understood now.
a720u10-jun23-12-q: Here, and in responses to Question 13, we found some of the worst examples of asserted biographical facts and connections made between the poets on the basis of their personal histories rather than their work. There were long, disconnected and often inaccurate accounts of the poets’ relationships, beliefs, sexuality and personality flaws. In one extreme case, candidates had learned ‘equivalences’ between characters or voices in the poems and real people. All circumstances in the poems were asserted as being ‘real’ e.g. the couple talking in bed are Larkin’s parents trapped in their miserable marriage; ‘Arnold’ was Larkin’s assistant librarian at Hull and ‘Havisham’ is a portrait of Duffy after she was deserted by Adrian Henry. It is understood that candidates will access independently study aids which might take these mistaken approaches to writing analytically and comparatively about poetry but centres are urged to do everything they can to redirect candidates’ interests and energies into the study of the poetry itself. It was sad to see that in their eagerness to repeat biographical gossip, many candidates had ignored the potential usefulness here of poems such as ‘An Arundel Tomb’, ‘MCMXIV’; ‘Nostalgia’ or (surprisingly) ‘Stafford Afternoons’.
a720u10-jun23-13-q: The comments for Question 12 above apply just as relevantly here. However, there were some excellent responses to this question many of which showed a keen appreciation and understanding of the illuminating differences between the ways in which Larkin and Duffy present their fellow humans. Weaker responses tended to stick firmly to an assertive line that Larkin is both a snob and a pessimist whereas Duffy is much more a poet in sympathy with her subjects. The tendency to approach poetry in this way possibly comes from an over-eager tendency to define poets’ ideas and attitudes in line with narrow expectations and miss the nuances that make the work worthwhile. A common feature which often compromised responses was the frequent and unqualified use of ‘positive’ and ‘negative’ when writing about attitudes which made for broad and assertive rather than analytical writing.
a720u10-jun23-14-q: Very few responses to this question were seen. The challenge was really to organise thoughts and responses relevantly and coherently across a very broad range of possible choices of text. Candidates could have chosen any area of human experience (passion; loss; domesticity and so on) but the temptation to narrate and assert aspects of biography was too much to resist in some cases. It is very important to emphasise that work under AO3, if it is to be valid and effective, must be closely linked to analysis (AO2).
a720u10-jun23-15-q:
This question gave an opportunity for candidates to debate the view expressed and balance different aspects of the poets’ work with the focus firmly upon the ‘presentation of different kinds of relationship’. It is always worth stressing that candidates are entitled to take issue with the critical views expressed in questions and they might, in this case, have made a strong case for ‘nature’ being ‘at the heart’ of Heaney’s and Sheers’ poetry rather than relationships provided they had given due critical attention to both the range of relationships and the ways in which they are presented. Once again, the danger here was an over-emphasis upon narrated biographies. Examiners who marked this response draw attention for the need to focus more precisely upon the connections (AO4) between the poets’ work.
In both responses there tended to be unrealistic claims for some of the technical aspects of the verse. There might be a case for connecting Sheers’ use of tercets to one of the nine or so verse forms in Welsh poetry but the point would need to be made in the light of the set task and in the course of close analysis. It would have been more profitable to concentrate upon the poets’ language choices rather than identifying and labeling devices or verse forms as outlined in the first point considered in the table in the overview to this component.
Summary of key points: • Teachers responsible for delivering both English Language, English Language and Literature and English Literature at A level should be sure that language used in the different classrooms and in practice written work meets the specific demands of the subject. The discussion of poetry in the English Literature classroom should concentrate upon vocabulary choices, implicit meaning, tone, auditory effects, imagery and literary devices such as metaphor, simile, hyperbole and so on. Most importantly, when making use of the technical terms from the literature ‘toolbox’, candidates must make sure they are not simply feature-spotting but analysing how such features function in making meaning. • Specific work needs to be done in many cases upon the development of range and precision in candidates active vocabularies. In the past, teachers have devised vocabulary-based word games at the introductory stage of lessons where the focus and content of the lesson is anticipated. This hardly needs explaining, but if a poem of a certain sort will be the focus of the lesson, then candidates might be invited as a starter to develop as much vocabulary as possible out of the key word ‘sad’ for instance, leading them perhaps to miserable; gloomy; wretched; desolate; dejected and so on. Discussions about nuanced differences and the emotional ‘temperature’ of words will be greatly beneficial. The important thing is to raise awareness of the importance of demonstrating clear engagement when writing about poetry through effective word choices. • There are useful materials available on the WJEC Eduqas subject-specific website which will help students to see the differences between descriptive writing, commentary and analysis. A failure to write analytically is the primary reason for depressed marks in this subject.
17 • Take care that well-intended support for students does not produce an over-rigid approach to the examination so that candidates are unprepared to interpret the specific demands of questions and to respond freshly and relevantly. • Candidates should be dissuaded from attempting to include every fragment of critical comment they have learned in the course of study. Exercises designed to help students apply what they know about other interpretations relevantly, and to provide examples of the development of critical discussions would be of great benefit. • The same applies to contextual knowledge. The key is to be found in whether or not a contextual reference can be connected to the ways in which the poet makes meaning. In other words AO2 and AO3 should be seen as bonded elements. Assertion should be discouraged and the presentation of simple equivalences between poetry and the real lives of writers i.e. “this is about a time when x did y” should be discouraged. • Make a point of showing how AO2 and AO4 should be combined in a kind of ‘double helix’ when it comes to making connections between the work of different poets. Dissuade learners from combining AO3 and AO4 as in all but the very most capable hands this approach will not allow the candidates to address AO4 (‘Explore connections across literary texts’) with any success. • Be cautious when identifying prosodic features; avoid both feature-spotting and unrealistic claims for the ways in which such features contribute to meaning.
Finally, as always, congratulations to teachers and candidates who have overcome all manner of difficulties to complete courses and to achieve levels of success which, in the very best performances, are genuinely humbling. Good luck with preparations for 2024 and I hope that at least some of the advice above might help candidates working at all levels to give of their best when the time comes.

a720u10-jun24-01-i: Some candidates resorted to describing Placebo’s behaviour rather than looking at the ways in which Chaucer presents the character. Analysis of presentation involves an examination of factors such as sequencing; use of direct speech; repetition of key words and phrases (“deere” and “brother” for instance) and the coherence of the character’s words, which, taken all together, seem to demonstrate the poet’s intentions in bringing the reader to an understanding of Placebo’s character. In many cases, candidates took this approach, thereby demonstrating their understanding and appreciation of literary concepts. Those who took a narrative or descriptive approach, sometimes filling-out their responses with contextual detail and / or inappropriate linguistic terminology, were not able to score well on this question.
a720u10-jun24-01-ii: Most candidates understood how Chaucer’s presentation of relationships between the sexes and between masters and their servants might well have involved a satirical, perhaps semi- serious undermining of the social order. Many responses were well-organised, building upon the presentation of sycophantic and disloyal service seen in the presentation of Placebo and moving on to look at Damyan and May with sensible glances at the world of the supernatural. Less successful responses became bogged-down in the presentation of the Merchant in the General Prologue and (much more surprisingly) in lengthy speculations upon Chaucer’s own unhappy marriage and his arraignment for ‘raptus’. Candidates must be reminded that Component 1 does not provide an opportunity for generalised, biographical journalism.
a720u10-jun24-02-i: There were some excellent analyses of both form and content here and the ways in which both the structure of Donne’s verse and his use of language / imagery presented his attitudes to both earthly and divine love and the ways in which the two became intertwined and mutually illuminating. Those who were tempted to give an account of Donne’s marriage and bereavement in place of critical analysis lost the opportunity to score well.
a720u10-jun24-02-ii: As is clearly apparent in the successful, opening to an essay on ‘worship / keen intellect and profound feelings’ above, many candidates who had studied Donne were very successful in coming to terms with this question and demonstrating a genuine understanding and enjoyment of some very complex verse. Weaker responses relied heavily upon snippets of biographical gossip and broad assertions about the culture of Donne’s period. Those who had come across critical observations on Donne’s qualities as a metaphysical poet mostly made good use of them. Even then, however, the stronger responses could have made a greater effort to discuss the relevant critical quotations which they had used.
a720u10-jun24-03-i: There were some very strong and sophisticated responses to this task showing a clear understanding of the effects of imagery and Milton’s exploitation of all five senses. There was also some perceptive analysis of the techniques of building atmosphere and establishing implicit meaning through patterns of language. Weaker responses described the extract and / or made far too much reference to other parts of the poem and consequently lost focus.
a720u10-jun24-03-ii: Milton seems to be more popular as this specification ages and candidates clearly enjoyed debating the issue of the presentation of blame in Book lX. The strongest responses linked Milton’s poetic techniques and use of language with the ways in which blame was implied, while weaker essays relied too heavily upon lengthy descriptions of context and abstract debate about blame rather than focusing upon the text. As with Chaucer and Donne, weaker candidates had far too much to say about Milton’s marriage which distracted them from literary analysis.
a720u10-jun24-04-i: Once again, we saw some very strong responses which were confident about the effects of structure, image choices and language patterns. Some correctly observed rhetorical devices and showed how these served the poet’s perceived purposes; less successful responses concentrated on identifying declaratives and interrogatives without further, analytical comment or analysis.
a720u10-jun24-04-ii: Most candidates avoided the trap of claiming within the introductory paragraph that other factors than “the desire for social justice” were the driving force of Blake’s poetry but for those who didn’t, this is a good opportunity to remind candidates that, in tasks of this sort. the view expressed in the question must be given due consideration before an alternative is suggested. Candidates made reference to a wide range of poems but there was an obvious preference for ‘London’ and the Chimney Sweeper poems. Weakness appeared when candidates seemed determined to answer on the presentation of children or relationships rather than social justice. Once again, the fewer references to Blake’s marriage and irrelevant but juicy biographical detail the better.
a720u10-jun24-05-i: Strong responses were preceptive in showing the effects of language in establishing distance and silence as powerful means of emphasising absence and therefore loss. Some candidates offered a general commentary on what would have been a well-studied poem without taking account of the focus of the question, which is ‘loss’, and consequently failed to score as well as they might have done with a better-planned response.
a720u10-jun24-05-ii: Ideas about death and the afterlife were seized upon with relish by most who attempted this question and there was some high-quality analysis of a range of relevant poems. A few responses drifted into the presentation of sin, weakness and women but most remained relevant. Contextual reference to Rossetti’s religious faith was obviously in order but, in some cases, this opened a floodgate with a rush of lengthy considerations of Rossetti’s charity work and her status within the Brotherhood. Please see the notes above on the judicious use of context. It is quality and relevance which counts, not quantity.
a720u10-jun24-06-q:
While not a very popular choice, Eliot’s and Hardy’s poetry has clearly provided a great deal of interest and enjoyment for many highly committed learners. Responses to Question 6 about connections between the ways in which the poets “write about their worlds” in the light of their suggested pessimism were thoughtful and often very sophisticated. The best essays did not lose sight of the satirical and / or dark humour which underpins the poets’ pessimistic attitudes, while strong but perhaps less sophisticated writing concentrated almost exclusively upon the disgust, contempt and weariness expressed in ‘The Waste Land’ and Hardy’s poems of 1912.
A similarly talented cohort of candidates responded to Question 7 and found much to disagree with in the set task. While most agreed that the poets did appeal to us differently, candidates did not necessarily accept (after due consideration) that the difference lay in the contrast between Hardy’s heart and Eliot’s mind.
14 Cleverly constructed arguments sometimes drew our attention to human qualities and respect (love for fellow man?) to be found in Hardy and a flintier approach from Eliot – possibly based in intellectual and social snobbery – so not quite hearts and minds, but close. It is good to see candidates (who understand the need to follow the rubric) with the confidence to take an individual approach.

Much of what has already been said in Section A about AO1, AO2, AO3 and AO5 applies to Section B too. However, by way of general comment it was noted in many cases that candidates did not seem to make best use of the 60 minutes suggested for this part of the paper. This was particularly apparent in those who chose to begin the examination with the Section B response. This is not against the rules of course, but it might have some bearing upon a widespread tendency to unload huge quantities of unfiltered material without adequate planning or due regard to the demands of the question and (as already mentioned) the need to focus the essay on poetry rather than biography or contexts. This becomes especially apparent in candidates’ attempts to address AO4 through comparisons of the poets’ lives or personalities rather than through their work.
13 Successful Responses:
• planned coherent, relevant and well-organised responses and selected at least two poems from each poet for close analysis • understood the need for sustained comparative analysis in the light of the task • made use of relevant contextual detail beyond consideration of the lives of the poets • understood that connections between the poets should be on the basis of how one poet’s ideas and techniques illuminate a reading / understanding / appreciation of the other • made judicious use of critical quotation. Below is an example of an opening to Q10 which suggests a successful trajectory for this kind of response:
‘In a poem of quite startling violence, Ted Hughes records the aggressive power of thistles as they “spike the summer air” and with images of splintered weapons”, “Icelandic frost” and buried warriors he observes the irrepressible cycle of rebirth as the dead plants, like dead men, are replaced when their “sons appear”. Plath also recognises the aggressive power of plants but in a different way as she loads the gift of tulips with sinister qualities, and they become representative of a world she wants to escape with their “dozen red lead sinkers round my neck.” and the ways in which they “eat my oxygen”.’
Less successful responses:
• offer poorly planned, overlong responses with little regard for the set task • work through a very limited range of poems descriptively and asserting meaning • offer extended and asserted accounts of poets’ lives • attempt to connect by comparison or contrast facets of the poets’ lives • make use of pre-learned critical quotation without regard to relevance. Below is a less promising response to Q10:
‘Silvia Plath had to spend time in hospital after an operation for appendicitis (or a miscarriage caused by Ted Hughes’ abuse – critics disagree) when her family sent tulips to her hospital ward which she describes as having a very negative power over her. Ted Hughes who was brought up in the Yorkshire countryside and had a fascination for the natural world also wrote about plants (thistles) which were powerful and negative like Vikings.’
• Candidates should aim to write shorter, better planned and more relevantly focused responses. • AO2 with its double weighting should drive the response throughout its length. • Judicious choices of relevant context should be used sparingly and exclusively to support analysis; biography should be de-emphasised. • Connections should be established on the basis of ideas and poetic technique and not upon similarities or differences in poets’ lives. • Pre-learned critical commentary on poets should be used with great discretion and only in support of relevant of textual analysis. What critics have had to say about poets’ lives is not a different reading rewardable under AO5.

Examiners understand that with this particular pairing there is a very strong temptation (particularly when it comes to a confessional poet in the Lowell tradition, as many candidates point out) to see the poems exclusively through the lens of the poets’ relationships. However, in some whole centres this tendency has reached extremes so that there is often only a bare minimum of attention to the ways in which meaning is made in poetry and how the works of one poet connects with the other, and instead candidates offer reams of asserted biographical detail. Once again, a reminder that the title of this Component is Poetry seems appropriate. Candidates must not be allowed to believe that pages of biographical gossip, often disconnected from any consideration of the poems, can earn credit. That said, there were some good examples of well-informed writing about different sorts of power in Question 10 with some subtle dimensions including the power of delusion and the power which the past exerts over the present.
While most of the points above apply equally to Question 11 on the poets’ ability to “transform the ordinary into something of extraordinary significance” it did attract slightly more analytical responses, although the popular choices of ‘You’re’ and ‘Full Moon and Little Frieda’ did tempt candidates into lengthy and only very loosely relevant biographical / contextual writing.

Larkin and Duffy remain almost as popular as Hughes and Plath in this section and Question 12 on “the observation of trivial detail which is most moving and evocative” produced some excellent responses. Candidates fully explored the impact and significance of a wide range of imagery from ashtrays in ‘Mr Bleaney’ or “That vase” in ‘Home is so Sad’ connecting to the telling domestic details in ‘Litany’ or the jukebox in ‘Never Go back’. Although this will sound a little like a stuck record on the same jukebox, many candidates could not resist the opportunities to write extensively about the lives and loves of the two poets. Again, this is more evidence that attention needs to be redirected on to the poetry itself and the ways in which meaning is made.
The invitation to explore comparatively the presentation of “relationships between people” in Question 13 gave candidates an opportunity to examine a variety of relationships rather than exclusively romantic attachments. Sadly, this opportunity was not taken up by many candidates whose responses remained limited to accounts of both poets’ love lives with a wearying emphasis upon Duffy's change of sexual preference and Larkin’s repeated betrayals of the women in his life. There was a great deal of ill-informed assertion here but those who went beyond ‘Talking in Bed’ or ‘First Love’ and looked more analytically at poems such as ‘An Arundel Tomb’ or ‘Broadcast’ along with ‘Moments of Grace’ or ‘Before You Were Mine’ were able to demonstrate more depth of understanding and appreciation.

a720u10-jun25-01-i:
Candidates were asked to “Examine Chaucer’s presentation of May” in lines 976-999 and most showed some grasp of the requirement to explore technique i.e. structure, tone, language choices and imagery which would lead a reader to an understanding of Chaucer’s intentions. Those who wrote generally and warmly about May’s deceitfulness or, alternatively, simply declared her a feminist heroine missed opportunities to write analytically about Chaucer’s poetic techniques.

Often students of Blake are defeated by the apparent simplicity of the poems and are thrown back on to relatively basic ideas about “nursery rhyme” structure or rhyme schemes. Better responses explored Blake’s technique in presenting a complex religious vision involving the fusion of the human and the divine with careful analysis of language such as “heart”; “face” and “dress”.
As we know, a successful address of AO3 involves demonstrating an understanding of the “contexts in which literary texts are written and received.” In many ways there could not have been a better opportunity to address both the “written “and “received” elements of this AO. As they considered the power and timelessness of Blake’s poetry, candidates had a clear opportunity to show how the implicit values in the poems were not restricted to any particular historical period but those who wrote extensively about contemporary society seemed to forget that literary essays must be led by AO2 and the analysis of poetry always needs to come first.

As we know, a successful address of AO3 involves demonstrating an understanding of the “contexts in which literary texts are written and received.” In many ways there could not have been a better opportunity to address both the “written “and “received” elements of this AO. As they considered the power and timelessness of Blake’s poetry, candidates had a clear opportunity to show how the implicit values in the poems were not restricted to any particular historical period but those who wrote extensively about contemporary society seemed to forget that literary essays must be led by AO2 and the analysis of poetry always needs to come first.
a720u10-jun25-05-i:
A line-by-line analysis of poems at this level will rarely produce a well-focused and relevant response. In this case, the task required an analysis of Rossetti’s presentation of “intense feelings” and it would have been wise to have started with an overview of the dominant mood, and tone of this poem which becomes apparent in “I cannot reach”; “Beyond my range”; “all in vain”; “strain”; “stretch” and finally a glimpse of redemptive “hope”. While there were some complex and sensitive responses, those who concentrated solely on structure, rhyme scheme and repetition of the first-person pronoun were not able to make a success of this task.
SECTION A (ii)
Successful responses: • took careful account of the specific demands of the questions • showed a clear intention from the start to analyse text • gave careful attention to the structure and coherence of essays • made relevant and economical use of contexts (please note “close reference” does not mean over-extended narrative accounts dislocated from textual analysis • incorporated relevant suggestions for different interpretations of poems into their own discussion / analyses.
Less successful responses: • failed to demonstrate engagement with relevant texts • relied upon raw biographical data and broad contextual “facts” with little or no direct application to tasks or texts • lacked coherent structure and development • repeated pre-learned critical views without attempts to apply them relevantly • described poems and asserted meanings.
Strong responses to this task (and there was a good number) acknowledged that much of Rossetti’s poetry might have a particular resonance for the religious reader but went on to argue convincingly that there was a great deal of her writing which could appeal to those who did not share her religious faith. This was a very sensible approach to a “How far do you agree?” style of question and there were some excellent responses which demonstrated confident ideas about the possible aesthetic appeal of the technical aspects of her poetry (religious or otherwise), as well as non-religious subject matter or cultural and social values which might be found universally appealing. It was pleasing to note the wide range of material which candidates drew upon.
SECTION B
Successful responses: • planned coherent, relevant and well-organised responses and selected at least two poems from each poet for close analysis • understood the need for sustained comparative analysis in the light of the task • made use of relevant contextual detail beyond consideration of the lives of the poets • understood that connections between the poets should be on the basis of how one poet’s ideas and techniques illuminate a reading / understanding / appreciation of the other • made judicious use of critical quotation.
Less successful responses: • offered poorly planned, overlong responses with little regard for the set task • worked through a very limited range of poems descriptively while asserting meaning • offered extended and asserted accounts of poets’ lives (for AO3) • attempted to connect by comparison or contrast facets of the poets’ lives (for AO4) • made use of pre-learned critical quotation without regard to relevance.

a720u10-jun25-06-q:
The best responses to Q6 concentrated upon the ways in which the two poets influence or manipulate reader’s feelings and ideas through their choices of subject matter and poetic techniques. The discussion should have paid due attention to whether or not readers could find any comfort or consolation in the poems and what connections could be made between Eliot’s and Hardy’s ideas and techniques. There were some expertly argued responses but those who did not perform as well had not really used the question to structure their responses and instead offered a general commentary on their selection of poems. The weakest responses spent far too much time on observing parallels in the poets’ lives, especially their marital relationships.
At the core of Q7 is the matter of objectivity and the presence or otherwise of “personality” in the poetry which affects the ways in which human subjects are presented. Some well- informed responses showed a confident awareness of Eliot’s stated ideas on this matter and were sensitive in their analysis of Hardy’s guilt-driven accounts of his grief and regrets. There was also some excellent analysis of Eliot’s presentation of society in poems other than ‘The Waste Land’ and in both poet’s presentation of the shaping influences of religious ideas.

a720u10-jun25-08-q: It was encouraging to see some very well-informed responses to Yeats and Abse. For Q8, most candidates performed strongly under AO3 and many found some imaginative ways of shaping their readings of both poets to the demands of the task- i.e. the debate about the main strengths of both lying in their qualities as storytellers. Some who seemed very keen to answer on the presentation of Irish and Welsh cultural history managed to turn their material into dealing with the ways in which the poets presented the “story” of Ireland and the “story” of Wales. Only a very few engaged in the debate by holding up storytelling against other possible strengths of both poets.
a720u10-jun25-09-q: Q9 was the more popular of the two questions on these poets and candidates showed a keen awareness of the connections between the mutually illuminating ways in which poems dealt with different varieties of love. It was encouraging to see how wide-ranging many of the responses were, taking-in romance, patriotism, familial ties and friendships. Weaknesses became apparent when candidates indulged in over-long descriptions of Yeats’ frustrations with Maud and Abse’s grief over Joan’s death, forgetting that responses need to be driven by an analysis of the chosen poems.
a720u10-jun25-10-q:
Many responses to Q10 were damaged by lengthy and descriptive biographical writing with only passing references to the poems themselves. With these two poets in particular, candidates must avoid the temptation to unpack all they know about the lives and personal suffering of the unfortunate pair. Certainly, in confessional poetry particularly, biography has a place in establishing relevant contexts but assertive claims about the relevance of poems to certain events in the poets’ lives without due consideration of what connections could be made between the poets in the ways in which they present “death” made for low quality responses.
Very much the same points as those made above could be made again here for Q11. That said, it was pleasing to see the subtlety with which some approached “landscapes”: the most adventurous looking at the highly imaginative elements of Plath’s poetry as well as the precision with which both poets create mood and atmosphere in the ways in which they “make use of landscapes”.

a720u10-jun25-12-q: In their response to Q12, candidates needed to demonstrate their appreciation and understanding of the ways in which human emotions are presented or implied by both poets in complex and nuanced ways. There was some excellent writing on this topic with confident analyses of poems such as ‘Talking in Bed’ and ‘Havisham’ with candidates showing a genuine understanding of how a reading of one poet could illuminate and inform a reading of the other. Once again, over-emphasis of biographical detail led some candidates astray. It is always the poetry which leads the way.
a720u10-jun25-13-q: Q13 was a very popular task where a good number of candidates showed an excellent appreciation and understanding of the ways in which humble or ordinary objects or situations could be imbued with such profound significance. Weaker responses tended to list examples of “minor details of domestic life” without showing how “curtains, thin and frayed” which fall “within five inches of the sill” or “One second hand bed” could be made to reveal such profound truths about human lives. Under AO4 it is vital to make connections between ideas and poetic techniques rather than simply similarities in subject matter or the details of the poets’ lives.
a720u10-jun25-14-q:
While there was not a large number of responses to these two poets, Q14 proved popular amongst the small sample and was generally very well done. Candidates ranged widely in their selection of material to demonstrate the poets’ “intense awareness of the physical world” and there was some confident writing about the ways in which both Heaney and Sheers linked their observations of the material world to more abstract and complex issues such as love, grief or regret. In some weaker responses, there was a hint that candidates were attempting to re-apply what might have been a practice essay on “landscapes” which limited the depth and coherence of their writing.
There were some enthusiastic responses to Q15 which aimed to demonstrate how “emotionally engaged” both poets appear to be. Lower performing essays did this mostly through assertion and appeals to a common understanding of the effects of love, bereavement, separation and so on. Better essays took a similar route but showed how emotional engagement was demonstrated through literary techniques. Only the strongest successfully tussled with the distinction in the task between emotional engagement and sentimentality. Those who appreciated that sentimentality (which tends to be a superficial quality) was avoided though the poets’ choices of language, tone and imagery when dealing with emotive subjects were most successful here.
Once again, a sincere thanks to teachers for their hard work in delivering this component and congratulations to those candidates who seem to have profited so highly from their study of poetry.

a720u10-oct20-14-q:
Both tasks were quite well addressed with some detailed and well-informed writing on both poets. As with all other texts in this section, there was a tendency to inject passages of barely integrated biographical writing into responses. There was also clear evidence of engagement and enjoyment which was very encouraging.
Summary of key points
• In Section A Part (i) responses, it is important to focus upon poetic technique. Description is not a valid substitute for analysis and candidates should always ask themselves HOW a poet is making meaning and (in order to show engagement) to what effect. • Points of view in Part (ii) questions must always be considered (AO5), not simply re- stated or rebutted without careful exploration. AO3 elements (contexts) must be used as part of a relevant analysis of the poet’s work so that essays remain literary rather than historical or biographical. • When selecting poems (or extracts from narrative poems) for consideration in Section A Part (ii) and Section B responses, choose on the basis of maximum relevance to the task rather than personal preference. • Connections (AO4) in Section B must be seen as opportunities to hold poems up against one another – comparisons or contrasts between the lives of the poets is of very limited value.
• Candidates should remind themselves of the differences between descriptive/narrative approaches and analytical writing. Please see WJEC resources on the appreciation of prose of poetry where the differences are clearly exampled and explained.

a720u20-jun17-01-i:
Most candidates engaged with Shakespeare’s presentation of Cordelia in this extract, but not all realised that France is part of the equation, missing the opportunity to discuss how he is used to add to her characterisation. Those who did seize the opportunity sometimes misinterpreted France’s attitude to Cordelia as one of hostility, describing him as shocked by her behaviour rather than by Lear’s behaviour.
Candidates generally grasped the conflict between Rome and Egypt in Antony’s characterisation and discussed how the other characters in the extract are used to sharpen this aspect of Antony’s presentation. Others saw how Antony is both defensive of his own actions and partly willing to ‘play the penitent’. Honour was a familiar concept to most, as was the tension between Caesar and Antony.
Most candidates engaged with certain aspects of Hamlet’s thoughts and feelings in this extract, notably his grief over his father and his plan to check the veracity of the ghost, revealed at the end of the extract. However, several struggled to grasp the situation of Hamlet’s confiding in Horatio, valuing his friendship and acknowledging his composure, and there were resulting difficulties in discussing what Hamlet was talking about. In many responses Horatio did not feature at all in their analysis of Hamlet’s thoughts and feelings in the extract and there were many misinterpretations of ‘my soul….mistress’, taking the mistress to be usually Ophelia/ Gertrude and ‘pregnant hinges’ persuading many that this was evidence of such a reading.
Most responses engaged fully with both Miranda’s and Ferdinand’s presentation, but there were a few who ignored Prospero’s contribution to the meeting. The concept of love at first sight was frequently mentioned, with some cynical of such a phenomenon, but generally Miranda’s awe and Ferdinand’s reciprocal admiration were grasped. Some of those who saw the role played by Prospero in the presentation of the two lovers thought Prospero was being sexist and misogynistic in calling Miranda ‘wench’.
a720u20-jun17-01-ii:
There was plenty of lively debate regarding the presentation of the three sisters as clear exponents of both good and evil, with most prepared to consider an alternative argument involving the male characters as equal or better illustration of the conflict, as Cordelia is absent for much of the play. The more discerning candidates embraced the concept of ‘primarily’, and some did considerable justice to the idea of Lear himself illustrating best the conflict between good and evil, with close analysis of the role of the Fool in association with that idea. Some argued that Goneril and Regan were not necessarily evil but the victims of Lear’s misogyny.
11 2. Antony and Cleopatra
Most candidates seemed engaged with the ideas and beliefs attributed separately to Rome and Egypt and were ready to discuss these in the context of whether sympathy was engendered for one set of values or both. This was usually in close examination of their relevance to the portrayal of the characters of Antony and Cleopatra themselves. There was also some careful discussion of Caesar and Enobarbus.
3. Hamlet
There was a variety of responses to this question, ranging from those who debated only whether Hamlet was a ‘victim’ to those who gave full consideration to the notion of ‘helpless’ and ‘world around him’. In general there was plenty of sensible discussion regarding Hamlet’s responsibility as an avenger and also a son, with the world around him variously defined as the royal court, the Ghost, Claudius, with Gertrude and Ophelia also brought into the discussion as arguably ‘helpless victims’ themselves. Some argued cogently that Hamlet was as much a victim of his own character and beliefs as the world around him, while others proposed that he was a helpless victim of the Ghost’s demands.
4. Henry IV Part 1
Too few responses to this text were seen for adequate comment.
5. The Tempest
There was an encouraging amount of lively debate in response to this question, with detailed consideration of the island setting, Prospero’s magic and the contribution of Ariel and Caliban. Prospero’s relationship with both of these characters was a popular avenue to explore, with several asserting that while his relationship with Caliban was realistic in terms of master-servant, his paternal relationship with Miranda was very much idealised. Others focused successfully on the minor characters and argued that their exchanges while under Prospero’s spell were very realistic.

General comments
Although there were instances where candidates had not thought first before tackling this section, it was encouraging on the whole to see very well planned and well structured responses. Better responses came from candidates who had clearly been prepared for targeted discussion of connections (AO4) and it was evident they knew this AO was double- weighted. In some instances AO4 proved tricky as candidates did not seem equipped to do the kind of comparison of texts that has so many marks attached to it. Those who used points of comparison as a planned approach were most successful.
Although the Malfi/Streetcar pairing was the predominant choice, it was encouraging to see centres taking on Doctor Faustus/Enron (which proved to be very productive) and also Lady Windermere’s Fan/Betrayal. Revengers/Loot produced some really excellent responses.
While it is impressive that candidates can press every relevant AO button in their responses several times, it is worth remembering that their comments on the text itself are of paramount importance, and there were instances of very able candidates discussing contexts and critics extensively, almost in a vacuum, mentioning the text only fleetingly before rushing on to make sure they press another button. AO3 and AO5 should be addressed in an integrated approach, and can only be rewarded fully where the discussion enhances that of the text in response to the question.
Question-specific comments
Marlowe/Prebble
There was some thoughtful engagement with Question 6, where there was evidence of detailed knowledge and understanding of morality play conventions, and interesting discussion of ideas such as over-reaching, greed, conceit and corruption. The more popular question was Question 7, with a range of definitions of greed and also some thoughtful engagement with ‘moral compass’, taking in the connections/contrasts between the corrupt business world in Enron and the corrupt individual egotism in Faustus. However, there were instances where candidates had not thought about any kind of greed other than that for wealth.
Webster/Williams
This text pairing was extremely popular, and although both questions were well represented, it appeared that Question 8 was the most popular question in the section as a whole. Many candidates seemed to agree that both central protagonists are equally victims and agents of their sexuality, so leading to their respective forms of ‘destruction’, while others debated
13 whether it was arguably more a case of their being just victims of male sexuality. It was encouraging to see so many candidates engaged with dramatic techniques and staging in particular, and it was also gratifying to note that in most cases the treatment of both plays was evenly balanced, with careful consideration given to both plays in responding to the view in the question.
A variety of approaches was even more noted on Q 9, where the word ‘disordered’ seemed to open all sorts of doors to really interesting analysis. There was some fruitful comparative discussion of ‘violent’ which again elicited some focused analysis of staging and other dramatic devices, while the concept of ‘cruelty is commonplace’ was either ignored or embraced as a given in the separate worlds of both plays. More discerning responses engaged with the suggestion of ‘commonplace’, arguing that both worlds reflected the overturning of established norms of behaviour, leading to a frightening acceptance of violence.
Middleton/Orton
Both questions were popular with those centres which had studied this pairing. There was plenty of engagement with the unsettling aspects in both plays, particularly in respect of the presentation of death and sexuality, and again there was an encouraging focus on staging and dramatic conventions. It was also evident that most candidates had been prepared well in terms of understanding dramatic genre and giving consideration to audience reaction. Those who chose Question 11 engaged with several reasons why both plays qualified as ‘serious drama’, such as the depiction of rape, and promiscuity, as well as the challenges presented to authority and authority figures, and as one candidate put it ‘the scrutiny of family values across both plays’.
Wilde/ Pinter
Both questions proved popular with those centres which had studied these texts. In Question 12 there was evident engagement with the concept of dishonesty in both plays, although some equated dishonesty with immorality in general. In these instances most ignored the view of ‘everyone attempts not to be understood’, while the stronger responses incorporated their consideration of this view into their discussion of characters’ dialogue, noting Pinter’s particular interest in elliptical conversations as opposed to Wilde’s carefully observed hypocrisy in social situations. In response to Question 13, there was some assured writing on Wilde, with detailed knowledge of the accepted social behaviour and in particular etiquette, but some more varied and less confident approaches to ‘manners’ in Pinter. However, morality was addressed equally in both texts, with some interesting discussion of the impact of the retrospective structure of Betrayal on the perceived immorality of Jerry and Emma. There were also some interesting responses where the attitudes towards women were carefully examined, and declared to be similar in both superficially different societies.
Shakespeare/Hare
Too few responses to this text pairing were seen for adequate comment.
14 Summary
Some issues to inform us all going forward:
 candidates should take time to consider what the question is asking, and also try to identify where assessment objectives are targeted in the question. It was a matter of general concern that in some centres it was clear to see that candidates were unaware that they had to address AO3 in both essays, and that this was double weighted in Shakespeare. …

a720u20-jun18-01-i:
Most candidates engaged with Shakespeare’s presentation of Lear in this extract. The majority noted his mental instability, anger and distress and that he is reacting to the storm on the heath. Fewer engaged with Lear’s thoughts on justice, or saw that he was imagining criminals, perhaps in response to his own feelings of injustice at the hands of his daughters, but it was encouraging to see candidates at least engage with the pattern of imagery relating to justice/crime/sin. The better answers argued that the ‘dreadful summoners’ are the elements of the storm calling the guilty to account in Lear’s mind. Most were able to discuss the key lines where Lear declares himself ‘more sinn’d against’ and that his ‘wits begin to turn’. The latter line was interpreted as either turning towards more composure and sanity, as he develops a concern for others, or turning into full-blown madness. Those who were secure in their reading of this extract were aware that Lear is accompanied by the Fool as well as Kent, and were able to interpret accurately the compassionate questioning in Lear’s last lines.
Some noted the impact of Kent’s speech in presenting Lear was to remind the audience and Lear of his vulnerability and the situation he finds himself in, a victim of the ‘hard house’. Some also noted that Kent’s deferential language ‘Gracious my lord’ reminds Lear of his former status and also confirms the respect he still engenders in his loyal followers.
a720u20-jun18-01-ii:
There was plenty of lively debate regarding justice in the play, though the issue of whether the audience is left ‘clearer about what is unjust than what is just’ was not always tackled or even acknowledged. It is important that candidates engage fully with the view given in the question.
Many discussed Lear, Gloucester and Cordelia as the best examples of unjust treatment, while there were many engaging arguments concerning Edmund’s candidacy for an ‘unjust death’ on the grounds of the ‘social injustice’ of his illegitimacy. Those who focused only on events missed the opportunity to discuss key speeches in the play which pertain to the issue of justice. Too many candidates spent rather too long on the opening scene, using it in some cases as their only source material for constructing an argument. Shakespeare’s use of the pagan gods and the idea of fate/destiny was explored in some cases, with productive results. One candidate argued that Gloucester’s blinding was ‘fate acting as a quasi-vigilante avenger’.
a720u20-jun18-02-i:
This extract enabled candidates to engage with Antony’s thoughts and feelings in reaction to having been told about Cleopatra’s ‘death’. Some candidates were unaware of the dramatic irony and did not appreciate that Cleopatra is still alive at this point. Most were able to engage with Antony’s despair and his suicidal thoughts, although fewer appreciated Eros’ role in his planned demise or understood that suicide presented the most honourable means of escaping his ignominious fate in Rome at the hand of victorious Caesar. Antony’s reference to ‘dishonour’ was sometimes wrongly attributed to the earlier battle and so some argued that he was still angry with Cleopatra instead of admiring her courage in taking her
12 own life and preventing Caesar from parading her as his spoils in Rome. The imagery of military honour was discussed as indicative of Antony’s moment of anagnorisis as he reflects on the glory of his past achievements with his ‘sword’ and ‘ships’ in contrast with his present decline, expressed through the imagery of ‘shame’ and ‘baseness’ in his imagined scenario in Rome. Only a few candidates discussed the impact of Eros’ reaction to Antony’s request in terms of how his strongly expressed reluctance colours the presentation of Antony as a whole, confirming the loyalty he inspires in his servants and followers.
a720u20-jun18-02-ii:
Most candidates welcomed the opportunity to discuss ‘personal conflict’, some only briefly engaging with ‘political’. Fewer engaged with the idea of ‘dramatic appeal’ and it is important to remember that questions often have a number of elements to address within the expressed view. It is not advantageous to focus on only one aspect and ignore the others.
Stronger responses argued cogently in favour of either the dramatic appeal of political or of personal conflict, usually citing sound evidence from the text and supporting their argument with other interpretations. Antony and Cleopatra’s relationship was explored from both sides of the argument, as being key to the concept of conflict. In some cases there was some good discussion suggesting that the personal and the political are so intertwined by Shakespeare that it is difficult to decide which is more dramatically appealing. It is important that candidates remember that this is a play and that they should give consideration to dramatic techniques as well as language in addressing A02. It is also worth remembering that general discussion which skims over the play’s events/narrative cannot be rewarded in the same way as textual analysis.
a720u20-jun18-03-i:
This question produced a variety of approaches to ‘parents’, with some considering Hamlet’s attitudes to his stepfather Claudius as well as to Gertrude and King Hamlet, while others discussed only his attitudes towards Gertrude and Claudius. There were many instances where candidates ignored Hamlet’s dead father altogether, despite the many references to him in this extract. The majority, however, concentrated on Gertrude and King Hamlet.
Most candidates grasped Hamlet’s anger at his mother for marrying Claudius as the chief aspect of the presentation of his character here. Some noted the disgust directed at his mother’s sexual relationship with Claudius as being the chief object of Hamlet’s fury, expressed through the use of ‘act’ and ‘deed’ and the animal imagery of ‘feed’ and ‘batten’, coupled with the insult ‘You cannot call it love’. Very few grasped the meaning of ‘judgment’, sometimes attributing it to God and retribution instead of Gertrude’s common sense.
The antithetical imagery in the first speech was discussed well by some candidates, with almost all engaging with ‘blister’ as connoting disease/infection in contrast to the ‘rose’ image of love and beauty. The best responses
13 were able to move beyond the narrative and focus on the key speeches where we see the conflict between both roles presented to the audience. Candidates who were fully aware that this exchange is after the wedding masque were better able to engage with the meaning of Prospero’s speeches. The opening aside was taken to indicate Prospero’s private concern regarding the threat of Caliban along with his expressed hatred for the ‘beast’, with the dismissal of the spirits which quickly follows showing his usual authority. Stronger responses noted the function of Ferdinand and Miranda in this scene, some seeing them as ‘foils’ in terms of their newly-wed happiness and concern set against the troubled and introspective Prospero. As both convey their surprise at the perceived change in Prospero’s behaviour, many saw this as a useful indicator to the audience that some transformation in Prospero is imminent.
Most were able to engage with the philosophical and introspective musings in Prospero’s monologue, but more secure readers were able to see the references to both the masque as the ‘revels’ and the possible implied reference to Prospero’s own art or indeed Shakespeare’s in his final play. Some, usually weaker responses, took the reference to Prospero’s ‘old brain’ in conjunction with ‘weakness’ literally and thought that this confirmed his senile dementia.
a720u20-jun18-05-ii:
Most candidates were able to produce an engaged response with the second half of the given view in the question, discussing characters in particular and sometimes ‘situation’, although some failed to consider the first part at all, missing the opportunity to discuss ‘a series of conjuring tricks’ as being the essential ‘dramatic action’. As noted in the general advice, it is important to engage fully with the question view. This is designed to enable candidates to begin to address AO5.
Stronger responses considered the use of magic as an inherent feature of characters and their relationships, discussing Prospero and Miranda’s relationship being one of control and dependency, Ferdinand and Miranda’s relationship as being illusory and Prospero’s relationship with Caliban showing the worst features of colonialism. Others wrote engagingly about the comic effects of conjuring tricks with the behaviour of the minor characters, while there were some interesting analyses of the opening shipwreck scene.
a720u20-jun18-06-q:
It was encouraging, on the whole, to see once again very well planned and well-structured responses to the essay questions in this section. Better responses came from candidates who had clearly been prepared for targeted discussion of connections (AO4) and it was evident they knew this AO was double-weighted. Those who used points of comparison as a planned approach were most successful.
Although the Malfi/Streetcar pairing was the predominant choice, it was encouraging to see more centres taking on Doctor Faustus/Enron and also Lady Windermere’s Fan/Betrayal. Revengers/Loot produced some really excellent responses, as was the case last year, and there were some equally strong responses to Measure for Measure/ Murmuring Judges despite this pairing being less popular.
While it is important that candidates must clearly address all the assessment objectives in their response, their comments on the texts themselves are of paramount importance, and there were instances of candidates discussing contexts and critics extensively, mentioning the text only fleetingly. AO3 and AO5 should be addressed in an integrated approach, and can only be rewarded fully where the discussion enhances that of the text in response to the question.
Marlowe/Prebble Both questions were popular. There were some excellent responses to Question 6, where well informed candidates analysed the significance and dramatic contribution of the various types of theatrical spectacle and argued convincingly for its role in creating the ‘intellectual substance’ of the plays. Others briefly engaged with the spectacle and moved on to discuss the plays’ essential concerns with overreaching and the consequences of pride. Stronger responses discussed the impact of Enron’s theatrical devices and produced astute arguments, some noting more contrasts than comparisons between the staging of the two plays.
a720u20-jun18-07-q:
Question 7 encouraged some candidates to make use of 21st century context, where one enterprising response drew analogies between Skilling, Faustus and the creator of Tesla cars as over-reachers, suggesting that testing the boundaries of knowledge can be intrinsically immoral. Most, however, took the opportunity to discuss how ideas about knowledge are presented in both plays, and made sound cases for connections, finally agreeing that morality issues were intertwined with the acquisition and application of knowledge.
Webster/Williams This text pairing was extremely popular, and although both questions were well represented, it appeared that Question 9 was the most popular question in the section as a whole.
In responding to the view in Question 8, candidates were required to engage with three concepts: boundaries of acceptable behaviour/unequal society/changing society. It was regrettable that in several instances candidates only wanted to discuss ‘unequal society’, seizing the chance to talk about ‘patriarchal societies’ where female characters were oppressed, usually for their sexuality. It is important to give careful consideration to all elements of the question, particularly where the question framing asks specifically ‘how far would you apply this comment’. Candidates must resist the urge to adapt the question to respond on the one aspect they hoped would come up.
A similar pattern emerged in response to Question 9, where some missed the word ‘reputation’ entirely and just wrote about attitudes to women. Stronger responses did justice to the whole question, giving some consideration to Ferdinand’s words in connecting both plays. There is a tendency to generalise when making contextual points about the different
15 periods, with sweeping assertions made about men returning from the World War II to perceptions of all women seen as a lesser species in Jacobean England. Better approaches carefully argued the differences between Blanche and the Duchess in terms of their social standing and reputations, also seeing the similarities between the attitudes and behaviour exemplified by Stanley, Mitch and Ferdinand. Female sexuality was a popular source for debate with many finding connections in the oppressive treatment suffered in both plays by the female protagonists.
There was a great deal of impressive referencing and quoting verbatim in support from both plays, with some producing excellent analysis of language and imagery patterns across the texts.
Middleton/Orton Both questions elicited strong responses, with candidates engaging fully with the opportunity to discuss the ‘bleakness and pessimism’ of both plays in Question 10, as well as base desires. There were strong responses where the comedy in Loot was connected with the darkly comic aspects in The Revenger’s Tragedy to present a counter argument to the given view. It was encouraging to see so many responses analysing imagery and staging closely and productively. It is also good to see candidates discussing the contextual influences of dramatic genres.
In responding to Question 11, candidates did more than justice to the issue of ‘no respect’, mining both plays for plentiful examples of this, but also acknowledging the black comedy as well as the macabre element in the use of the body/body parts as props.
Wilde/ Pinter Both questions proved popular with the increasing number of centres which had studied these texts. It was encouraging to see many candidates integrating contextual discussion into their arguments, sometimes using contemporary facts/statistics or literature of the time to support their points. Even those who wandered down the well-trodden ‘biographical’ path used their sources wisely.

There was a tendency to ignore the ‘superficial society’ in weaker responses, and this affected their response adversely. Some also considered the inflexibility of other individuals, such as Isabella, and whether this was a strength rather than a criticism.

Question 15 encouraged candidates to focus on how the law is presented as deceitful in both plays, and those who tackled it did justice to both texts, in some cases arguing that the justice figures are themselves flawed in terms of their personal morality, rather than the institution itself. Attitudes towards females in both societies were explored in the light of what many argued were patriarchal societies.
Summary Candidates and teachers need to remember that above all examiners look to reward engagement with the texts and all discussion of contexts and other interpretations should be properly integrated into the response, not merely acknowledged or invented, as appeared to be the case sometimes. As noted last year, there is evidence of some groups of candidates adopting a ‘one size fits all’ approach to contexts and critics, with the same material offloaded regardless of the question. It is only the most astute of candidates who can turn this around to their own advantage.
Finally, the team of examiners for this component wish to congratulate all candidates and their teachers for a most encouraging response to this paper. This is a demanding component which tests knowledge and understanding of three plays, without the texts for reference, and with double weighting of AO3 and AO4.
We have been privileged to read so many interesting and genuinely academic responses to these texts.
Please note that more feedback will be available in the autumn series of CPD and we very much hope teachers will be able to attend.

a720u20-jun19-01-i:
In Section A, King Lear and Hamlet remain the most popular texts, with The Tempest quickly building its popularity profile every year. Antony and Cleopatra and King Henry IV Part 1 are less popular, but it is rewarding to see that both plays are clearly stimulating and rewarding for those candidates who study them.
In response to the Shakespeare extract, candidates were often clear in their knowledge and understanding of the chosen part of the play and were reasonably accurate in discussing, for example, Lear’s state of mind/the presentation of Cleopatra or Falstaff/the relationship between Prospero and Ariel. However, there was some uncertainty regarding ‘Hamlet’s thoughts about himself’, with a preference for describing feelings rather than considering how Hamlet’s thoughts are presented by Shakespeare. Those who missed the reference to Fortinbras struggled to access the second half of Hamlet’s soliloquy, and there were several who misinterpreted the ‘eggshell’ concept.
In response to the Shakespeare essay in part (ii), there were several different approaches to the issue of sanity/madness in the King Lear question, with the more successful responses engaging with concepts of Lear’s actual madness, the ‘professional madness’ of the Fool and the feigned madness of Edgar.
8 Those who argued for the madness of Edmund, Goneril and Regan sometimes struggled to develop sufficiently coherent arguments, especially if they had not tried to define the characters’ behaviour as a kind of madness at the outset. Most saw the case for Cordelia’s sanity being the most apparent, with some suggesting that in her sane rejection of the love test she demonstrated a kind of madness in refusing a slice of the kingdom and its associated security.
It is worth remembering that candidates must pay close attention to the wording of questions in Section A part (ii), so that, for example, in attempting the Hamlet essay question, ‘obsession’ with honour cannot be overlooked as a ‘driving force of the play’. Some discussed the revenge tragedy genre, with many willing to consider the different kinds of honour in the play, for example attitudes towards female chastity. The strongest responses avoided narrating contexts but interwove them skilfully into their central argument. It was pleasing to see that the CPD message in recent years regarding the worth of literary /ideological contexts has borne fruit, and there were many instances of responses which were pleasingly tuned in to concepts rather than just historical events.
The Tempest question produced some impressive work on ideas about freedom and oppression, with a clear focus on key relationships and especially ideas about colonialism. Those who wrote on Antony and Cleopatra engaged with the question of dominant power and argued convincingly for the dominance of either Egypt or Rome, the popular approach being a study of the central relationship and Cleopatra’s sole claim to the power of Egypt through Shakespeare’s characterisation and themes. Although Henry IV Part 1 is still very much a minority choice, the essays produced on the court and tavern as opposing worlds were generally stimulating and well supported, with some interesting scrutiny of the differences in how Shakespeare constructs dialogue, including the impact of blank verse versus prose.

a720u20-jun19-07-q:
In Section B, the most popular text pairing by some considerable distance remains that of The Duchess of Malfi /A Streetcar Named Desire, but Doctor Faustus/Enron was also a popular combination for study. It is pleasing to see all texts attempted on the paper.
Examiners were impressed by the capacity of candidates to write focused, planned, cogently argued and well supported essays in this section, with accurate and apt quotations impressively integrated. It is also to be noted how well prepared centres are for this section in particular. The candidates’ evident enjoyment of the texts is a genuine reflection of not only their own endeavour but also their teachers’ hard work in preparing them and engaging them.
a720u20-jun19-08-q: Question 8 was the most popular question in this section, with many interesting discussions on the insecurity of males, although there was a temptation to focus on the powerlessness of females exclusively in terms of sexuality.
a720u20-jun19-09-q:
Question 9 produced some thoughtful work on confined locations and destructive impact, and it was pleasing to see close scrutiny of stagecraft and dramatic technique in response to this question.
9 Question 10 was significantly more popular than 11, with responses fully engaged in the elements of both plays which qualified for mock and shock, some arguing that in neither play was the social criticism served up a healthy dose. It was very pleasing here to see the candidate’s knowledge and understanding of different dramatic traditions and conventions put to good use.
Questions 12 and 13 seemed to be relatively evenly attempted, both offering the candidate the opportunity to discuss attitudes and values within the respective cultures and contexts. There were some particularly thoughtful responses to the idea of self-betrayal, and some close attention to the insights which might be gleaned.
Finally, questions 14 and 15 seemed to attract quite an even spread of responses, with clear engagement with ideas about public and private morality and the system of law favouring the rich. It is interesting to see how these plays in particular stimulate candidates’ sense of injustice and inequality, and examiners saw many responses which showed a high level of engagement with ideas about systems and organisations as presented in the two plays.
Summary of key points
• It is important to remember to read the set extract from the Shakespeare play as closely as possible, without attempting to respond immediately to the question. • It is also important to engage with all elements of the essay questions, as they offer a critical view which must be addressed during the course of the response. • Too many essay responses are over-long and consequently unstructured, with some barely coherent. Expression skills are often severely compromised when candidates are rushing to pour out all their knowledge, sometimes irrespective of the question. This should be discouraged. Examiners frequently saw 6-8 pages written in Section B, and this is unnecessary. Please remember that it is quality not quantity which is valued. • Where poor handwriting impedes the legibility of a response, it makes awarding a mark very difficult. Many responses this year might have fared better if they had been word processed. WJEC has clear advice on applying for this facility.

There was some good focus on the language and imagery in part (i) and some close reading, although there was frequent misidentification when candidates attempted to use grammar terms (imperatives often described as declaratives; and terms like adjective and verb quite frequently misapplied). Some candidates dwelt on the presentation of Kent or Cordelia, without turning it to the focus of the question on Lear.
10 Part (ii) responses often made good use of tragic theory and its conventions, with the classical Greek terminology of hubris and hamartia etc. often well applied within a critical and contextual framework. Some excellent and insightful comments were offered on how the minor characters, such as the Fool, might complicate the reading presented in the question. Insightful and engaged responses were astutely aware of the contextual implications of this Jacobean play, although some candidates seemed to think he divided Scotland and England, not united them. Candidates often built fluent arguments around the elements they considered to be important in addition to the tragic consequences, thereby proving their case that it was indeed "more than" the question suggested, with good use made of the sub-plot and the characterisation of the evil characters (particularly Edmund) and the saintly Cordelia. Stronger responses offered links to other plays of the period and, in particular, other Shakespearean tragedies.

a720u20-jun22-02-i:
There was general sympathy for Antony in the part (i) question, with some recognition of the significance of Enobarbus’ contribution to the perception of Antony as a popular leader, first to Cleopatra in an aside and then to Antony when he makes the audience aware of the men’s weeping. Most saw the significance of Antony’s exhortation to ‘drown consideration’, and ‘Scant not my cups’, criticising him for poor leadership in failing to plan for battle and focusing on sensual enjoyment instead. Stronger responses included discussion of death and honour and showed awareness of Shakespeare’s presentation of some humility in Antony. Several merely used the extract to discuss Roman v Egyptian values.
The essay question proved widely accessible, with good discussion evident regarding the issues of weak leadership and ‘a great love story’, many seizing the opportunity to compare the two cultures of Egypt and Rome and to point out that Caesar was clearly the best leader. The idea of Cleopatra as also a leader was not commonly seen and there were missed opportunities to discuss relationships between leaders and those they lead. Some saw the love as merely lust while others thought it is clearly a love story but not a ‘great’ one.

a720u20-jun22-03-i:
The famous soliloquy in part (i) gave the candidates plenty to write about, so the best responses judiciously selected key ideas with an eye on the overall shape and progression of the argument. Most candidates could identify some sense of struggle, though only the strongest were able to tease apart the detail of the scene and assess Hamlet's fragmented state of mind. The best also related the thinking neatly to "this point in the play", placing it on a dramatic arc; some less secure responses were a little confused about where it occurred or considered it just to be about the contemplation of whether or not to kill Claudius. There was some very effective analysis of imagery, Hamlet’s focus on death and the presentation of his private questioning, the fragmented nature of thought conveyed by caesura and enjambement. One memorable response argued that when Hamlet fears the ‘undiscover’d country’ he is suffering from a case of ‘destination anxiety’!
The part (ii) question invited thoughtful agreement and disagreement, with some of the best responses again informed by the notion of a tragic hero, informed by Aristotle, and also in some cases a sophisticated consideration of the revenge tragedy as a sub-genre. However, too many concentrated on the notion of Hamlet simply being ‘disappointing’ to audience and other characters alike, and some unfortunately took the given view as an invitation to discuss whether Hamlet is a ‘hero’ in the broadest possible and least literary sense. In some instances the issue of ‘lacks pride’ was simply ignored, although the better-informed candidates were happy to take the opportunity to discuss pride within the tragedy genre.

a720u20-jun22-04-i:
There were very few responses to this text.
Most were able to identify the extract and position it at the correct point in the play and in the plot. They perceived the King’s angry contrasting of his son Harry with the ‘infant warrior’ Hotspur and the frustration and clear disappointment of the King with regards to his son and heir’s behaviour in this speech. They were able to analyse the language with its focus on military but also emotional language and terminology, and they were able to fully understand and analyse classical references.
Similarly, for part (ii), most of the responses were at least appropriate, with a good portion of them being secure and confident. Most identified that the end of Part 1 is a turning point for the character of Harry and made appropriate reference to the tavern episodes and Falstaff's influence. They were able to analyse the psychological complexity of Prince Hal and his evolution as a character up until the moment when he turns into a heroic figure in helping the King control the rebellion.
One concern regards the sparseness of contextual references. Most references were to the contemporary political scene and some to actual performances. a720u20-jun22-05-i:
This text is proving to be increasingly popular. The part (i) extract offered good scope to compare the presentation of Prospero in his final dramatic interaction with other characters – particularly Alonso and Ariel in the extract – and then his contemplative address to the audience. A few weaker candidates were less secure on the switch and misread some of the Epilogue as addressed to Alonso and/or all the characters, as if Prospero was asking them for forgiveness and release. Some good responses noted the effect of the switch to shorter, rhyming lines and the possible interpretation of Prospero as a controller, like a director or playwright, although the occasional diversion into biographical AO3 was not helpful on a section assessed for AO1 and AO2. It was pleasing to note, however, that most saw Prospero’s transition from magus to man and recognised the significance of his reference to ‘faint’ strength. While some saw him as striking a newly penitent tone, others noted he is shown as defensive about his ‘project’ which was ‘to please’ and that he never appears apologetic. Those who grasped the breaking down of the ‘fourth wall’ offered penetrating insight into the metatheatrical aspect of the epilogue.
The part (ii) essay was best dealt with when ‘moral’ centre was kept in the foreground, although several ignored or misunderstood the key word ‘moral’ and discussed only Prospero’s ‘centrality’ in the play as a whole. Fortunately, this usually led them to some consideration of his moral/immoral behaviour, but it is vital to engage with the whole question. Those who did focus on the whole question offered thoughtful discussion of the morality of the following: the treatment of Caliban and Ariel, including but not confined to colonial considerations; the controlling of Miranda and, to some degree, Ferdinand, including the position of women (and Shakespeare's daughter Susanna!) in society; different forms of magic; and the divine right of rulers, with Prospero's usurpation compared to the Gunpowder plot.
