a720u20-jun22-06-q:
Both questions produced some astounding responses that judiciously selected textual detail to enhance meaningful, convincing comparative arguments. Candidates seemed very well prepared for these texts and there was clear engagement with the similarities and differences between the use of power to corrupt in the two plays in Q6 and ideas about change in Q9. It was particularly rewarding to see so many engage with the texts as stage productions, with various dramatic devices in the two plays being used as the foundation for detailed discussion of the focused topics. Rich contextual material, especially for Enron, and also the morality play genre for Doctor Faustus, was in general carefully integrated into comparative consideration of different kinds of power and ideas about change.
Qs 8&9: The Duchess of Malfi/A Streetcar Named Desire The enduring popularity of this pairing of texts is clearly founded on most learners’ good grasp of the contrasting techniques, periods and a well-researched range of critical responses. Candidates excelled at Q8. It was a pleasure to see so many good scripts. Many obviously enjoyed analysing the loss of identity from so many different angles, including the loss of female identity under the pressure of masculinity and social expectations, but also the loss of male identity. Some of the scripts analysed the loss of social and political identity of most characters in relation to the historical context.
The expressed view gave candidates great scope to identify the ‘several angles’ of their choosing in the consideration of ‘loss’. Candidates interpreted the ‘loss of identity’ in interesting ways not only for Blanche and the Duchess but also for Mitch, Stella, Stanley, Ferdinand, Bosola, Julia. A variety of independent positions were adopted, frequently arguing that the Duchess maintained her identity whilst Blanche’s disintegrated.
In addressing AO3, candidates frequently made very detailed references to the social and political structure of the contemporary historical period and the impact that this was perceived to have on the characters. There were references to the American Civil War and World War II but also to the actual Italian contextual origin of the Duchess of Malfi with additional references to the contemporary English situation. In addressing AO2 many were able to offer analysis of the dramatic techniques used by both Williams and Webster and how they similarly re-visit traditional genres.
13 The key assessment objective AO4 was generally tackled very well, with so many similarities found between the plots and the characters but also striking differences. The characters of the Duchess and Blanche were mostly compared, but also Ferdinand and Stanley and other minor characters. Social and contextual influences and expectations were also compared and the impact of male hegemony in patriarchal societies. It was particularly rewarding to see full engagement with stage directions, as strong responses analysed the use of light/darkness, costumes, props and stage positioning. In addressing AO5, candidates showed strong critical engagement with various views, a range of feminist, Marxist, and Freudian approaches being the most common.

a720u20-jun22-08-q:
The following concerns need some attention: • Comparative analysis was often at an 'appropriate' level; unfortunately, some candidates resorted to a narrative-based comparison of the texts. • In addressing other views some candidates merely quoted a view without making use of it, or in the worst cases made up a comment in order to tick a box. These were often barely literate. • Candidates should remember that in studying these texts dramatic staging is significant; reading these texts as prose (without considering the elements of stage and audience) does limit the framework of sustained and meaningful comparative discussion. • Finally, it is in this section where we see the regrettable tendency to write far too much. Often candidates have achieved their marks after three sides of a page, but they persist in writing another three to four. In over-long answers candidates risk diluting the quality and compromising the structure of their response.
Summary of key points
• It is important to remember to read the set extract from Shakespeare as closely as possible, without attempting to respond immediately to the question. • It is also important to engage with all elements of the essay questions, as they offer a critical view which must be addressed during the course of the response. • Too many essay responses are over-long and consequently unstructured, with some barely coherent. Expression skills are often severely compromised when candidates are rushing to pour out all their knowledge, sometimes irrespective of the question. This should be discouraged. Examiners frequently saw 6-8 pages written in Section B, and this is unnecessary. Please remember that it is quality not quantity which is valued.

a720u20-jun22-09-q: Q9 was also a popular choice, with the destruction of family bonds explored well against various dramatic and contextual backgrounds that explored the ‘worlds’ of the plays and their lack of compassion or loyalty. Again, however, independent thought was much on show by candidates who offered examples of loyalty or compassion in both plays.
a720u20-jun22-10-q: This text pairing is clearly growing in popularity, and as we have observed in previous years, a high number of candidates in response to these plays produced scholarly, erudite responses which examiners can only marvel at and applaud. Many were able to delve into considerable textual detail in their comparative analysis of both plays, and integrate apt, pertinent critical views and valuable contextual and ideological insights to illuminate their arguments. It is always refreshing to see candidates who are confident in shaping their own critical views in response to the task, and who are fully able to discuss the texts in a ‘mature, discerning’ way. The strongest responses recognised the ‘carnivalesque’ genre associated with Q10’s ‘carnival of nastiness’ and argued cogently against the expressed view, discussing what else the plays offer, for example a strong critique of their respective societies and cultures. Q11 invited candidates to focus on how death is presented, and in response to this question we saw some particularly accomplished analysis of staging and props, with a sharply maintained focus on the audience at all times. The more discerning argued that we see only nihilism behind Orton’s play but some effort at retribution and therefore a more moral and instructive message in the events and characterisation of Middleton’s play. In responses to both questions and to both plays there was a sustained appreciation of farce and slapstick comedy.

In response to both questions, candidates engaged well with the central issues and had plenty to say about pretence and the destructive force of love in the plays’ respective societies and cultures. Several drew on biographical material for Pinter and Wilde, but not exclusively, and when used it was frequently pertinent to the discussion rather than merely narrated. It was pleasing to see some thorough examination of the different styles of dialogue, with contextual and critical references to dramatic genres, such as the Theatre of the Absurd for Pinter, and what has now become recognised as ‘Pinteresque’ dramatic technique with the judicious use of pauses. In Lady Windermere’s Fan, the tradition of social etiquette and the genre of melodrama were frequently referred to in Q12 and candidates were well informed about bourgeois culture and attitudes.
There was a clear awareness of different kinds of love in Q13, with close examination of maternal love and its capacity to destroy other relationships in both plays, with others positing that male friendship is presented, especially in Betrayal, as more valued and more destructive than romantic/marital love. Some candidates noted the lighter tone and use of humour in Wilde’s play in contrast to the intensity of the scenes in Betrayal, with one candidate noting sadly that love in Betrayal was a lonely business in comparison to the world of Lady Windermere’s Fan where it is regularly held up to scrutiny and gossip.

a720u20-jun23-01-i: Occasionally in the extract question, candidates made overinflated claims about the significance of one or both characters speaking in blank verse, as if this was a deliberate choice for these lines rather than the frequent choice for royal characters. (Of course, if more effectively contrasted with, say, the disjointed prose of Lear at other points, then a more valid point emerged.) Some candidates interpreted Lear as still mad or deluded to a degree that was unconvincing. Yes, he is unrealistically optimistic but the repetition of “No, no, no etc.” does not really represent a breaking down of his speech due to mental instability. Those who insisted he is mad at this stage were unaware of his arc in the play and had forgotten about the earlier scene when he awakes to find Cordelia and has his anagnorisis. Better answers saw the dramatic contrast between the pathos of Lear’s happiness and optimism in dire circumstances, and also the pathos of Cordelia’s practicality and realism. The best saw the dramatic function of Edmund in the extract as a reminder of the presentation of Lear and Cordelia as prisoners and their grim fate, and others discussed the terse, callous language of Edmund set against the lyricism of Lear. Further strong responses accurately interpreted the ‘gilded butterflies’ as the superficial courtiers of Lear’s past life as King, arguing that he is now able to distinguish between the trivial and the important.
a720u20-jun23-01-ii:
The question provided the opportunity for effective discussion, with some candidates arguing cogently in support of the division as a catalyst for the play’s suffering while others effectively considered the seeds of suffering in the Gloucester sub-plot, or other interpretations about a lack of empathy or family love being the principal cause of suffering.
There was some fruitful discussion of Shakespeare’s use of Greek tragedy features and some consideration of feminist criticism in relation to Goneril and Regan. As noted above, the ability to quote accurately and freely from the play was admirable and was a useful support for responses across the whole range of performance.
a720u20-jun23-02-i: Those who had read the play diligently were aware immediately of the reason for Octavius’ anger, and his sense of personal grievance that his sister had arrived back home without due respect and acclamation. Some candidates attributed to Caesar some mistreatment of his sister that showed a misunderstanding of aspects of the extract. He does not consider her a “market-maid”, for instance, but instead is outraged that her entrance was not heralded and she has been treated by Antony as an insignificant person such as a market- maid instead of his wife and Octavius Caesar’s sister. The strongest responses grasped the difference in characterisation between Octavius and Octavia, although also observing their close sibling relationship: several saw Octavia as quietly assertive, maintaining her sense of loyalty to both her husband and her brother, while others saw her as a victim of male arrogance. Many were interested in the use of hyperbole in the use of nature imagery.
a720u20-jun23-02-ii: The essay question was generally done well, with candidates engaging readily with the focus on some of the principal concerns of the play. Many argued cogently that the passion v reason conflict is best shown through the characterisation of Antony himself, with the best responses including a detailed analysis of Enobarbus’ personal conflict. Contexts were used well on the whole and Egyptian and Roman values were closely discussed in their interrogation of the play’s speeches and settings.
a720u20-jun23-03-i: While the question for part (i) does not specify that the scene must be placed in context, this was an extract that benefited from precisely that. Some candidates took Gertrude’s statements at face value; but a more sophisticated interpretation was informed by consideration of how she and Hamlet had concluded their dealings in the closet scene, and therefore how Gertrude chose to present her son to Claudius. Similarly, Claudius’ speeches were better considered in the light of his own duplicity and therefore gained resonance if viewed in the light of diverting guilt and attention from himself. Some candidates did not appear to recognise the use of the royal “we”, attributing meanings to statements concerning himself only that were thus less accurate when applied to the two characters of the scene as a couple (“It shall be laid to us…so much was our love”).Some responses viewed the extract as an example of joint parental concern, while the stronger responses saw Claudius’ ruthlessness , focusing on the irony of Claudius’ image of disease in relation to Hamlet, and Gertrude’s carefully chosen nature imagery to modify her presentation of Hamlet and allow the audience to see that she is carrying out Hamlet’s request in the previous scene.
a720u20-jun23-03-ii:
The part (ii) question’s critical view yielded rich scope for discussion, with family loyalty usefully applied to Gertrude, to Hamlet, to his relationship with Old Hamlet and the cause for revenge, to Laertes, to Fortinbras, to Ophelia and her obedience. The context of classical and/or revenge tragedy was usefully applied by many, with some good use also made of Protestant and Catholic attitudes to ghosts and/or purgatory, and some more tangential reference made to Elizabeth I’s succession. Some approached the question by exploring the disloyalty of Claudius to his brother, and Gertrude’s disloyalty to her husband's memory.
Those who discussed Hamlet’s disloyalty to Ophelia through his antic disposition in the ‘nunnery’ scene and to Rosencrantz and Guildenstern forgot the question’s specific focus on family loyalty. It was interesting to note that many candidates did not fully engage with the idea of ‘destructive’. It is important to consider all parts of the question, even though it is acceptable to prioritise one aspect over another.
a720u20-jun23-04-i: Most grasped the essence of Hotspur 's character and his attitude towards the Prince. Inevitably, candidates discussed the readiness to fight, his belief in the justice of his cause and his contempt for the wildness of Prince Hal. The stronger responses drew attention to the use of the Messenger who was seen as a necessary curb to Hotspur’s hot-headedness, reminding the audience also of the urgent military situation, whilst also noting that Hotspur’s florid/hyperbolic language exemplifies his love of chivalry and codes of honourable military conduct. Very few made use of the key word ‘Esperance’ in relation to this aspect. However, there was good discussion of Hotspur’s aggressive language as he anticipates the battle and his use of motivational language to rally his men.
a720u20-jun23-04-ii:
The essay question seemed to be accessible to all those who attempted this play. Falstaff as well as the Prince was seen as a useful subject for debating the subject of ‘sacrificing public duty’ for ‘personal desires’, with some detailed examination of his ‘honour’ speech and his contribution to the comic scenes earlier in the play. Others chose to discuss the King as a prime example of this critical view, using the rich material of the rebels’ speeches with their references to the King’s past behaviour as the usurper Bolingbroke, as well as the King’s speeches to Hal about his conduct in relation to King Richard as a contrary point of view.
Those who had given careful thought to the presentation of Hotspur in part i were able to argue cogently that Hotspur was less about public duty in his quest for conflict with the king, and more about a personal and family vendetta.
a720u20-jun23-05-i:
It was evident that some candidates missed the irony of Gonzalo’s speech, in that Sebastian and Antonio mock Gonzalo’s utopian vision as impossible. Many candidates, conversely, felt that the ‘Long live Gonzalo!’ and ‘Save his majesty!’ were genuine endorsements of Gonzalo’s vision. However, there were many who saw the contradictions in Gonzalo’s ideal kingdom and others who had plenty to say about the marginalisation of women. It was a pity that for several candidates who were less confident of this extract that there was little engagement in the comedy of the scene for the audience in terms of the situation and dialogue. Some candidates wanted to credit contextual influences in Montaigne, where they recognised it, although context is not credited as such in part (i); but more significant was perhaps the lack of focus in some answers on the presentation of Gonzalo, rather than simply the state he portrays. His character as a noble Neapolitan was sometimes ignored, along with his good intentions; and more could have been made by some of how he and his higher ideals are shown in the effective contrast with the cynicism of Sebastian and Antonio. Their contributions to the scene were ignored by some or taken rather literally as valid criticisms of Gonzalo - although the naivety of the latter was fairly claimed by some.
Part ii The part (ii) question was again an open invitation to discuss a range of possible aspects of the play, with useful contexts including colonialism – sometimes very relevantly applied, in criticism of Prospero or Caliban or both - as well as useful attitudes to magic.
23 It is entirely possible, as observed in some responses this year, for candidates to access the higher bands by delimiting their focus to a particular theme or idea. Indeed, streamlined and pointed essays are often more rigorously argued than those which attempt to incorporate everything the candidate knows about the play. The most erudite responses are judiciously selective in their material and use brief, well-explained quotations or support from the play to elucidate their analysis. Context will then deftly embolden this analysis. Rather than acting as a tag-on, candidates at the highest level interweave context where specifically relevant to the development of the argument. One of the strongest responses was seen to take Shakespeare’s use of the masque in the play as a central focus for discussion of the ‘negative view of an ideal world’ debate. The result was a sophisticated literary essay which seamlessly blended AO5, AO2 and AO3, drawing on literary traditions and genres.
In general, candidates examined the character presentation of Prospero as their chief way in to this central debate, and most argued that the control of Prospero was the key reason why an ideal world can never be a positive construct on the island.
a720u20-jun23-05-ii: The Tempest is growing in popularity with each year that passes. Some of the most sophisticated essays which examiners see in this section of the paper are in response to this play. This particular question gave opportunities to engage with concepts and contexts.
a720u20-jun23-06-q:
Both question choices invited candidates to think about important concepts in the plays, and there was a fairly even divide in choice between the two questions. Many considered all kinds of relevant boundaries, including religious/moral, rule-breaking, boundaries in regard to personal relationships, societal traditions and expectations etc. Many found plenty to write about in focusing on the main protagonists themselves, but also by offering insights regarding the minor characters and audiences of the different time periods.
Just as in Q6, Q7 required a close examination of the main protagonists in order to discuss the idea of ‘irresponsible’, ‘wrong’ and ‘regardless’ of consequences’, with many readily seeing connections between Faustus, Fastow and Skilling. It was pleasing to see candidates discussing connections between the playwrights’ deployment of stagecraft and spectacle, and also making connections with situation/circumstances and contemporary beliefs. It was also reassuring to see the morality play genre and traditions knowledgeably discussed, while the refreshingly different spectacles and stagecraft of Prebble provided for some thoughtful and genuinely academic debate.
24 Q.8/9 The Duchess of Malfi/A Streetcar Named Desire
In Q8, Blanche and the Duchess were often considered well in the light of the statement regarding outsiders, with familiar material still intelligently used in the light of this statement. Other characters also came under consideration, especially Bosola and, less often, Antonio but also, interestingly, Mitch and/or Stanley, depending on how the Old or New South were characterised. The statement “focuses exclusively” invited consideration of other useful elements; but the occasional candidate omitted to answer the full question (“the presentation of outsiders”), not the statement in isolation. There was good analysis of stagecraft and detailed discussion of Williams’ stage directions in presenting characters as outsiders. The Duchess was shown to retain her identity, despite her harsh treatment as an ostracised outsider, while most felt that the consequences of being an outsider from the outset caused Blanche’s disintegration. Many acknowledged that the Duchess is not technically an outsider although she becomes one, while Blanche is an outsider throughout. Social status, backgrounds and morality were mined thoroughly for contexts. There was a surprising amount of sympathy for Ferdinand in Malfi, especially regarding his lycanthropy, while some sympathised with Stanley who was also an ‘outsider’ in terms of his social class. It was disappointing that many candidates virtually ignored the ‘dare to be different’ strand offered as part of the critical view in the question.
In Q9, again, there were many possibilities in the answering of this question, weighing up physical abuse particularly – but not exclusively – as experienced by the female protagonists, and also the mental suffering of a range of characters, male and female. There was no right or wrong interpretation of which had the greater impact; but the best answers kept their eye on the dramatic presentation of these experiences, as all Section B responses should. So the wording of the statement, with its mention of “dramatic tension”, was sometimes very helpfully referenced by candidates who considered dramatic structure and techniques in the unfolding of the presentation. Stella and Mitch were interestingly considered in the light of mental suffering, for example, in their crises towards the end of “Streetcar” while, as noted in Q8, Ferdinand received some sympathetic discussion in view of his mental instability and his regret in regard to the Duchess. Stronger responses argued that the worst suffering was the threat of violence and the off-stage presentation of violence, particularly for the audience. As always, candidates were eager to discuss attitudes towards and mistreatment of women in both plays and there is plenty of evidence to find in regard of this aspect. The amount of perceptive, sophisticated analysis of language, dramatic techniques and imagery was astounding this year.

a720u20-jun23-10-q:
For both questions on this pairing, responses were frequently informed by apt context, perhaps more (and obviously so) in the question on religion than its counterpart. Candidates grasped the disturbing yet comical undertones of both Middleton and Orton’s texts. Astute analysis of the moral depravity of both plays was offered. For example, there were some intellectually stimulating arguments which hinged around the propensity (and indeed desire) for audiences to suspend their disbelief and willingly engage in the complex moral framework of the plays.
For Q10, candidates embraced the opportunity to examine the presentation of sex, lust, marriage and death in determining the argument of how both plays might please and repulse in equal measure. Both plays offer considerable support for both, with comedy, farce and black comedy being weighed up against disturbing scenes of cruelty/violence and careless disregard for the dead. There was some excellent discussion of stagecraft in both plays, and careful scrutiny of the different types of dialogue, the strongest able to see connections by virtue of characters’ attitudes and values, particularly in regard to the treatment of women.

a720u20-jun23-12-q:
Wilde and Pinter remain a less popular pairing but the readiness with which candidates found successful connections between the two plays continues to remind us of the rich possibilities that this pairing offers. They perhaps provide an accessible and arguably more focused pairing for some candidates. Frequent use is made of certain comments by Billington, which are helpful; but as noted elsewhere, the statements in both questions also give rich scope for AO5 argument.
Echoing observations made last year, examiners were thoroughly impressed by the responses to these texts. Evidently, candidates are working at a very high level when comparing Wilde and Pinter. These are challenging texts (as are all the other pairings on this paper), but responses were often argued with élan, and there was a consistently comparative focus on ideas of sexual morality and the presentation of women as powerless. Responses were often characterised by a sharp critical eye. Candidates, it seemed, were ever ready to tackle the foundation of the question itself. For instance, one argued in Q13 that women may well be powerless, but they arguably also establish the metrics by which they themselves are defined and so gain an indisputably strong sense of individualism in spite of the codes that society attempted to enforce.
Q12 provoked some good discussion of sexual morality, as specified in the question; often informed by the statement, although candidates made more of the “art of making conversation” in relation to Wilde (perhaps rightly). Good discussion was also had about fidelity to one’s partner, with some interesting argument that the most important fidelity in Pinter was in fact asexual (or at least, not consummated) in the friendship of Jerry and Robert.
a720u20-jun23-13-q: Q13 also elicited good discussion and the question’s reference to “society’s views” prompted more explicit AO3 consideration than perhaps was the case in Q12. Some of this remains rather generalised and stereotyped, particularly in consideration of women’s roles as house- keeper and child-rearer; this does not seem very applicable to the upper-class protagonists of Wilde or the working lives of the professional gallery-owner and doctor (offstage) in Pinter. Again, some candidates successfully argued against the statement while others endorsed it, for either one or both plays. It is the skill and evident knowledge with which they present their case that is assessed, with the examiner keeping an open mind. A candidate that takes time to plan and present an overview of their judgement at the start often writes a more convincing essay as a result. Candidates must be reminded that more than 4/5 pages is almost always too long. Cogency, coherence and organisation suffer as a result.
a720u20-jun23-14-q:
Very few centres study this pairing. However, those who did became thoroughly immersed in the task of discussing the abuse of power and authority in Q14 or society’s failure to break down intolerance and prejudice in Q15. One candidate wrote in response to Q14: ‘the plays both present how the authority system is in dire need of reform.’ Another reflected ‘how a lack of checks and balances’ lead to abuse of power/authority.
Examiners were impressed with how candidates showed their own concerns about power and authority from their own contemporary perspectives on society and their perceptions of those who have the power and authority to run it. The standard of discussion on these texts was consistently high, with most candidates showing an impressive grasp of concepts and issues, as well as a keen appreciation of the plays’ stagecraft and characterisation.
26 Summary of key points: • Encourage learners to think carefully about all aspects of an essay question, signalling to the examiner that they have done so, before choosing to focus their response on particular aspects. • Discourage over-long responses and encourage shorter sentences. • Candidates should aim for coherence and cogency rather than quantity. • Contexts are only useful if they support the point made or are helpful to the discussion of the question. Sweeping, uninformed statements about how people were treated in various time periods are of little consequence without specific examples. • Continue to encourage using literary/cultural material for contexts, making learners aware that other plays by Shakespeare are useful and specific sources. • Avoid using critical views if they are not relevant or especially if they are fabricated. Examiners would prefer to read candidates’ own critical discussion. • There is a worrying new trend towards analysis by narration/description. Please urge learners to avoid retelling the story, however beautifully and accurately. Examiners know the stories back to front!

a720u20-jun24-01-i: Candidates clearly engaged with this extract, finding much to say about the breakdown of the relationship between father and daughter. Many candidates began with Lear’s anger, with more developed answers exploring Goneril as both an estranged daughter and powerful female figure. Some were able to use Albany’s interjections, and Goneril’s handling of him, to shed further light on the presentation of her character.
a720u20-jun24-01-ii: There were many excellent responses to this question. Candidates enjoyed exploring a range of relationships which demonstrated ‘conflict between youth and age’, often building up to interesting and individual conclusions in their essays. The character of Edmund proved a particularly popular focus, resulting in good links to context. Some candidates took the opportunity to conclude that the youthful characters who are not in conflict with their elders provide the moments where the ‘play’s main appeal lies’.
a720u20-jun24-02-i: All candidates were able to engage with the ways in which Shakespeare presents Antony’s victorious tone and the recognition he wishes to bestow upon his men. Some of the more perceptive answers analysed how Anthony is caught here between militaristic triumph and emotional declaration, devoting considerable time to how Cleopatra’s character adds to the portrayal of Antony and the mood of the scene.
a720u20-jun24-02-ii: The essay question was generally done well, with candidates fully engaging with various moments throughout the play which provided instances of pathos, tragedy and humiliation. Many were able to draw upon the context of genre and used their knowledge of the conventions of tragedy to interrogate the critical view in the question, in a lively and scholarly way.
a720u20-jun24-03-i: There was plenty for candidates to engage with in this extract. Hamlet’s disgust was usually the starting point for analysis. A considerable number of responses were quite caught up in what was seen as Hamlet’s ‘obsession’ with Gertrude’s sexuality and sex life with Claudius. At times, this dominated at the expense of other elements of the dialogue. The stronger responses were able to appreciate Gertrude’s moment of self-awareness and also to see the maternal element within her lines. Less successful responses tended to assert that Hamlet was simply mad at this point in the play.
a720u20-jun24-03-ii: The Part (ii) question’s critical view was clearly one which candidates were well-prepared to engage with. Stronger candidates noted the concept of ‘fate’ in the view and used this to construct sophisticated arguments. Others focused firmly on the debate between ‘thought’ and ‘feeling’, linking their ideas to the essential qualities of Hamlet’s character. One very pleasing point was the range of textual support used for this question, with candidates being inspired to draw upon examples across the whole of the play and not just the most obvious scenes. AO3 was addressed very well and there was some scholarly engagement with the key ideas of the Renaissance and how these are reflected in the complexity of Hamlet’s character.
a720u20-jun24-04-i: There was some misreading of the extract, with a few candidates being unsure of the subject of the King’s speech. However, there was also some successful commentary on language and imagery and how this revealed the character’s ‘thoughts and feelings’.
a720u20-jun24-04-ii: The essay question was generally well answered, with a balanced approach to AOs. Candidates explored the ‘past’ as presented in the plotline of the play, but others also took a contextual angle and discussed the play as social commentary for the audience.
a720u20-jun24-05-i: Candidates had a secure overview of the relationship between Ariel and Prospero and were able to identify this extract as a turning point or shift in the character dynamics. A large number of candidates conflated part i and ii of the question and applied the ‘master and servant’ focus to the extract as well as the essay. In some cases, this led to a degree of repetition of extract material in the essay.
a720u20-jun24-05-ii: For this question candidates made very good use of the critical quotation in the question, beginning with analysis of Prospero and Ariel and then moving on to explore other relationships which present master-servant qualities. Prospero’s relationships with Miranda and Caliban were a rich source of discussion, with Post-Colonial and Feminist readings being fruitfully applied.
a720u20-jun24-06-q: Question 6 was marginally more popular, with candidates exploring a wide range of different kinds of ‘human weakness’, such as ambition, greed and selfishness. Question 7 provided a thought-provoking critical viewpoint and there were some excellent and impassioned responses which came to very different conclusions about whether the moral messages of the playwrights are undermined. Many candidates really engaged with the stagecraft and symbolism of both plays when exploring the ‘entertains’ element of the critical quotation.
a720u20-jun24-07-q:
Section B places considerable demands on the candidates in that all assessment objectives are in play. As noted earlier, AO4 is worth 20 marks and high-level comparisons need careful planning and development. The most common pitfall is where candidates make a link between the two plays and then move on to deal with each play separately, forgetting to return to the comparison point to develop it further.
The most popular Section B choice continues to be Malfi/Streetcar. The Faustus/Enron pairing is continuing to attract new centres and examiners saw some excellent essays comparing these texts.
a720u20-jun24-08-q: Question 8 was by far the most popular question. Some candidates focused only on sexual desire and others used the critical quote as a springboard to explore further ideas, such as desire for power, dominance or security. A number of candidates produced excellent answers linking desire to madness, which enabled productive comparisons between the plays.
a720u20-jun24-09-q: Question 9 was less popular but very engaging as there are so many elements of ‘false appearance’ and ‘deception’ in both plays. Some of the stronger answers were able to explore the way in which the playwrights elicit sympathy for certain types of ‘deception’ which are not necessarily morally wrong or malicious.
a720u20-jun24-10-q: There were some remarkable responses to this pairing of texts. Question 10 sparked sophisticated critical debate about how the audience’s ‘ideas and beliefs’ are challenged. Candidates were thoughtful about the context of reception and how audiences of different times might respond to the more provocative elements of the plays.
a720u20-jun24-11-q: Question 11, which asked about ‘preoccupation with the human body’ and ‘types of humour’, was less popular but no less impressive. AO2 was generally excellent as candidates were able to write eloquently about comic effect of both the slapstick and grotesque kind.
a720u20-jun24-12-q: Question 12 sparked some good responses and the focus on ‘relationships’ was open enough to allow candidates flexibility in terms of the relationships they chose to focus upon. Pinter’s play sparked interesting discussion of male friendship and parental/maternal relationships was another rewarding area which many chose to explore. Notably, AO5 was strong on both questions and candidates have clearly spent time studying critical opinions, using them intelligently.
a720u20-jun24-13-q: Question 13 asked about a ‘superficial society where respectability is more important than morality’. Candidates were able to construct convincing arguments and to interweave context skilfully. Pinter’s biographical context was popular for this question and ranged from simplistic comments about his affair with Bakewell to sophisticated understanding of the shifting moral codes of the time.
a720u20-jun24-14-q:
Very few centres study this pairing. Question 14, for which the focus was ‘ideas about dishonesty’, was the most popular. Candidates found plenty of opportunities to make connections between the plays and many wrote well on the moral implications of dishonesty. For question 15, candidates were able to link ‘social injustice’ to contexts and to explore other ‘issues’ presented within the plays.
20 Summary of key points: • Awareness of the heavily weighted assessment objectives in both sections should inform candidates’ planning of responses, so that these are an integral part of the essay structure and not simply added on as the candidate is writing. • Time should be taken to allow candidates to explore the difference between Band 3 and Band 5 performance in the heavily weighted assessment objectives in both sections. • Context (AO3) must always be firmly linked to the text to be productive. • Avoid essays which are too long. The strongest candidates are judicious in their selection of material and remain fully engaged and in control of their essay until the last word. • For Section B, candidates should avoid making a link between the two plays and then moving on to deal with each play separately. Good connections need to be developed. • Candidates should take some time to think and to plan their response carefully before they begin to write their response to the question.

a720u20-jun25-01-i: Most candidates grasped the circumstances of Gloucester’s blinding in this extract, and most were able to comment on Gloucester’s vulnerability and Regan’s cruelty. However, many were unable to see that Gloucester was not referring to himself but to Lear in his references to ‘his poor old eyes / his anointed flesh / his bare head / poor old heart / he holp the heavens’. Consequently, this common misreading missed Gloucester’s defiant loyalty to Lear and his compassion for his suffering on the heath at the hands of his daughters, and instead there were suggestions that Gloucester is self-pitying and feeble here. His brave attack on Regan and by extension Goneril, ‘I shall see / The winged vengeance overtake such children’ with its dramatic irony was not always grasped, and some candidates thought that Regan was calling Gloucester a ‘dog’ instead of the servant. The best answers made use of the servant as a foil to Regan in discussing how Regan is presented here, pointing out the second instance of defiant loyalty in the extract, this time to Gloucester. These responses also commented sensibly on Gloucester’s opening line as an example of his endurance and bravery, with Shakespeare’s use of animal imagery paving the way for the cruel suffering to come in this extract.
a720u20-jun25-01-ii:
In general, candidates engaged readily with this essay question and discussed fully the many examples of the play’s world as being ‘all dark and comfortless’.
Many argued that the blinding scene and the storm scene represented the best examples, while others began with the seeds of darkness and lack of comfort being sown in the opening scene. There were interesting angles explored, with the sub-plot’s parallelling of the main plot a popular route, as well as social considerations such as the treatment of the old and the poor and mentally ill in Edgar’s representation of Poor Tom. Some gave careful consideration to whether there were any redeeming features to the world created in the play, producing cogently argued discussions of the importance of Cordelia, Kent and the Fool.
Some made use of significant cultural context and religious context was also explored.
a720u20-jun25-02-i: Most candidates grasped Antony’s anger with Cleopatra here, but too many misunderstood the specific reason for his anger at this point in the play. Many assumed this exchange was straight after the point when Antony left the battle and chased after Cleopatra. Those who read the extract correctly understood that Antony is displaying as much jealousy here as anger, as he discloses the reason for his rage at Cleopatra after her question towards the end of the extract – he is in a jealous rage after seeing Cleopatra flirting with Thidias, Caesar’s messenger – ‘To let a fellow that will take rewards….be familiar with / My playfellow, your hand’. Once this situation is grasped, the attack on Cleopatra’s sexual experience and promiscuity makes clearer sense. However, candidates who missed this important trigger were still able to be rewarded for grasping that his attack on Cleopatra is sexually motivated, many pointing out the use of food imagery, ‘morsel’ / ‘fragment’, to demean her and trivialise her relationships with other famous lovers, with key words attacking Cleopatra’ s morality: ‘hotter hours’ / ‘vulgar’ / ‘Luxuriously’ / ‘’you can guess what temperance should be’ / ‘You know not what it is’. The word ‘boggler’ was generally understood as a comment on Cleopatra’s promiscuity and lack of dependability. Antony’s reference to the gods and their seeling of men’s eyes was taken by many as Antony trying to absolve himself of blame for his loss of judgement and ‘adoring’ his error. His use of ‘viciousness’ and ‘filth’ was seen as an awareness of his wrongdoing in partnering Cleopatra.
a720u20-jun25-02-ii: In general, candidates engaged well with the given view of the play. Many discussed fruitfully the differences between Egypt and Rome from the standpoints of both politics and love, while there were some very impressive explorations of Shakespeare’s imagery of ‘melting’ and dissolution as playing a pivotal role in the presentation of themes of instability / shifting sands. Strong cases were made for Cleopatra’s presentation subverting the audience’s expectations towards the end of the play as her stability as leader of Egypt leading up to her suicide contrasted with Antony’s perceived weak leadership as one of the Roman triumvirate and his instability as husband and lover. Many explored the idea of the stability of Octavius Caesar ‘s leadership and argued for his shrewd management of his co-leaders and common enemies. Some excellent analyses of Shakespeare’s presentation of the cultural ethos of Egypt were seen, with detailed and perceptive exploration of patterns of imagery in Shakespeare’s depiction of the Nile.
a720u20-jun25-03-i: Most candidates were able to grasp the situation here of a fencing match between Hamlet and Laertes. Those who read the extract closely were able to understand Shakespeare’s use of dramatic irony and explored how Hamlet may be presented as disingenuous, pleading forgiveness for his actions when he was not in his right state of mind- ‘His madness’ used as an excuse when the audience knows he adopted an ‘antic disposition’. Several also argued that Laertes is being equally disingenuous, as he has concocted a plot with Claudius to kill Hamlet during this fencing match, and so, of course, there is more dramatic irony. The more adventurous responses made use of the setting and stagecraft and also the use of chivalric language, with some ably discussing the performative nature of this scene, and the two sets of audiences. There was some good discussion of the different types of language used by Laertes and Hamlet to express their positions and emotions, and most commented on Hamlet’s repeated use of third person and the repetition of his name in asking for Laertes’ forgiveness. The word ‘brother’ was frequently discussed as an indicator of fellow-feeling for Laertes, and a possible reference to Hamlet’s hopes to have married Ophelia.
a720u20-jun25-03-ii: In general, there was purposeful engagement with the view in the essay question. Many agreed that Hamlet himself was his ‘greatest obstacle’, exploring key moments in the play, such as his reluctance to kill Claudius while he was apparently praying; killing Polonius; the closet scene with his mother and many others. A popular route into the question was through the soliloquies and many explored the significance of Hamlet as an overthinker. However, there were cogent arguments put forward regarding the role of the Ghost in the play and the difficulties of the task Hamlet was required to carry out. Contextual references to religion and cultural references to the Renaissance and the conventions of revenge tragedy enhanced arguments, as well as various critical theories and views of the play. Some candidates argued that Hamlet’s greatest obstacle is the corrupt court of Elsinore, analysing the presentation of the court throughout the play and using the presentation of Claudius as a key factor in the overall corruption.
a720u20-jun25-04-i:
The sense of the Prince’s transformation at this point in the play was noted by most candidates, with some grasp shown of Vernon’s high opinion of Harry set against Hotspur’s more cynical view of his enemy. – ‘challeng’d you to single fight’ / ‘Seem’d it in contempt?’
The stronger responses commented on the idea of honourable conduct as Vernon reports in eloquent iambic pentameter that the Prince praised Hotspur and showed ‘grace’, while also noting that the Prince is presented as a chivalric ideal here and a model prince, ‘became him like a prince indeed’. The patriotic fervour shown by Vernon was noted by some as an instance of dramatic irony in view of the coming battle, ‘England did never owe so sweet a hope’. Hotspur’s feelings about the Prince were seen as mixed, as he shares the Prince’s desire to settle the conflict man to man to save the deaths of many, while also making light of Vernon’s glowing testimony with the word ‘follies’.
a720u20-jun25-04-ii:
Candidates varied in their approach to the essay question. Although both strands of the view in the question were addressed, some preferred to discuss the transformation of the Prince, with less attention paid to Falstaff. Others opted to discuss Falstaff’s progress through the whole play, with attention more sparingly paid to Hal’s progress. The question focus of ‘wins our hearts and minds’ gave rise to a mixed bag of opinions, some seeing Falstaff as the real hero of the play, his humorous attack on ‘honour’ discussed as a valuable attribute in winning our minds, while others saw the pathos of his changed relationship with the Prince winning our hearts.
This play offers the chance for candidates to engage with rich contextual material, and it was pleasing to see that this opportunity was taken up by most.
a720u20-jun25-05-i: As noted in previous reports, some of the most sophisticated essays which examiners see in this section of the paper are in response to this play. Most candidates grasped Shakespeare’s portrayal of the two lovers declaring their love and admiration for each other, with stronger responses commenting on the courtly love theme in Ferdinand’s subservience as ‘log-man’. There were several who argued that Ferdinand appears to boast of his experience with previous lovers, with the repetition of ‘full many’ supporting this idea, but most agreed that his admiration of Miranda is without question, using the ’So perfect and peerless’ declaration as the best example. Some strong responses saw Miranda as bold and independent in her assertion that she would not ‘wish / Any companion in the world but you’ and also in her reference to her virginity ‘the jewel in my dower’ as an important virtue for any prospective husband. Others argued that she is still under Prospero’s rule as she reins in her love and admiration for Ferdinand at the end of her speech by reminding herself of her ‘father’s precepts’. Only the most discerning remembered that Prospero had made Ferdinand a ‘patient log-man’ as a trial of the young man’s love for Miranda and so were able to explore the contrast between his status as Prince with his now demeaning position in ‘wooden slavery’. The lyrical language in Ferdinand’s last speech from ‘Hear my soul speak’ was observed nicely, and there were no doubters of the love between these two characters. Others also explored Shakespeare’s use of iambic pentameter and shared lines as evidence of the positive portrayal of the lovers. However, several made the point that Prospero has orchestrated this alliance, referencing the metaphor ‘jewel’ as a reminder of the transactional nature of this relationship from Prospero’s perspective.
a720u20-jun25-05-ii:
The extract question is intended to offer a ‘springboard’ into the essay question and this year was no exception. Most candidates explored the relationship between Ferdinand and Miranda more fully in their essay, arguing that although Prospero’s scheming could potentially tarnish the love presented between these two, there was sufficient evidence that Shakespeare wants to see their love as meaningful and uplifting. The wedding masque was explored as a positive example of this love, as well as more detailed analysis of how Ferdinand and Miranda are presented at different points in the play. There was fruitful discussion of the father-daughter relationship, many reaching for Prospero’s declaration that everything he does is for Miranda. Most argued that this is a loving relationship, but some cogently argued that Prospero’s controlling character sometimes worked against this presentation. Love was explored more widely in terms of Caliban’s relationship with Prospero and Caliban’s evident love for the island. The Prospero-Ariel relationship was also examined as an interesting kind of love between master and servant. However, many argued that it is hate and revenge which dominate this play and that sibling love is absent between Prospero and Antonio, despite the play’s ending. Not many explored the idea of self-love in the case of Prospero.
19 SECTION B: DRAMA Candidates this year generally seemed better prepared for the management of the different AOs they need to address for this essay task. This was evident in the opening paragraphs where a brief engagement with all or some AOs was immediately evident. However, there is sometimes insufficient focus on the double-weighted task of making connections (AO4) and consequently vital marks are lost. It is important to answer the key aspects of the question. One question choice asks for a response to the stated critical view in terms of its application to both plays, while the other asks for candidates to explore connections with a given focus, ‘in the light of’ the stated view. Candidates sometimes spend too long on the stated view in the second question choice, examining it in detail rather than giving sufficient time for exploring the actual focus of connections.
The strongest responses came up with connections between the plays that were perceptive, sometimes surprising and original, and well-founded, as shown by developed AO2 analysis. The most popular pairing by a considerable margin is still The Duchess of Malfi / A Streetcar Named Desire, where again examiners were very impressed with the enthusiasm for both texts shown across the range of ability. Doctor Faustus / Enron, Lady Windermere’s Fan / Betrayal are continuing to attract new centres, and we saw some very thoughtful essays written on these texts, as well as on the other text pairings. Given that this paper examines only ‘closed book’ texts, it is remarkable how learners continue to analyse the texts in depth and detail, integrating relevant, sometimes illuminating contextual material and discussing other view of the plays with critical rigour, while tackling a question which asks them to compare two quite different plays.
a720u20-jun25-06-q: Those who attempted Q6 tended to either agree with the given critical view or disagree, arguing that the ‘primary’ focus instead is overreaching. Whichever approach was taken, most engaged with the idea of individual power being abused, the power of knowledge being a popular candidate focus, as well as the power of individuals within a broader framework such as the Enron corporation. Examiners saw plenty of good contextual discussion regarding the two different time periods and cultures, and this year candidates seemed very willing to analyse stagecraft and settings in depth and detail. There were very effective comparisons and also contrasts established, with several commenting that Faustus’ fate evokes more audience sympathy at the end than Skilling’s punishment as he was ‘under the control of Mephistopheles’ while Skilling was a completely free agent.
a720u20-jun25-07-q: Q7 gave candidates a specific focus in the stem of the question – ‘explore connections between…presentation of ideas about wealth’ – but some focused instead only on the initial quoted view. Many engaged with ideas such as the wealth of knowledge as well as material wealth and the wealth of self-gratification, ‘profit and delight’. Most seemed to see no value in the pursuit of wealth and explored the contextual backgrounds for confirmation that both central characters would find no support for their actions and beliefs from their respective worlds.
a720u20-jun25-08-q:
Both questions were equally popular. Q8 responses generally agreed that key characters were vivid and memorable but seemed less keen to explore the ‘lack of morals’ angle. Candidates understandably explored familiar territory such as attitudes towards female sexuality, and there were the usual frequent references to ‘toxic masculinity’. Both of these avenues were productive in discussing the morality/immorality of Blanche and the Duchess, but many argued that the Duchess’ morality was not in question, only when judged by the moral standards of her own society, while Blanche’s promiscuous behaviour, especially with the young boy, was universally condemned. The Duchess of Malfi text was forensically examined for evidence of not just immorality but amorality, and it was pleasing to see the rigour in textual analysis for this play this year. Every year we see impressively detailed analysis of A Streetcar named Desire, and this year those standards were maintained, with a more focused approach this year to the stagecraft and settings of both plays, which led to productive connections (AO4). It was also encouraging to see how purposefully contexts were used to support arguments, many pointing out the importance of religion as well as social class for Malfi.
Some of those who chose Q9 spent some considerable time discussing the quotation in detail, and spent a little less time on the actual question focus of the presentation of ‘ideas about illusion and reality’. Consequently, too much time was spent comparing and contrasting the ‘unforgiving, harsh society’ in both plays and too little on the explicit connections focus of ‘ideas about illusion and reality’. However, there were many excellent essays in response to this question, as candidates argued that dreams/illusions are integral to the situation of entrapment which Blanche and the Duchess both find themselves in within their very different time periods. Contrasts were found between the two heroines and their desires/dreams, with many noting that in Blanche’s case, her dreams are rooted in the privileged past of Belle Reve, while the Duchess’ dreams are rooted in the future with her husband and children. Examiners saw very pertinent and well-crafted arguments regarding Blanche’s illusions about herself and her Southern Belle identity, comparing her reactions to adversity at the close of the play with the Duchess’ dignified and stoic behaviour at her end. In general, candidates across the range of ability were able to discuss stagecraft, setting and dialogue in detail, and there was a sharper focus this year on other critical views of the plays. Cultural context in particular featured in an increasing number of responses this year, and most worked hard to integrate this into their central argument. However, we are still seeing some very brief engagement with contexts, where only sweeping assumptions are made about attitudes towards women over time and about women’s actual lives during the relevant period.

a720u20-jun25-10-q:
Once again this year, examiners were treated to some excellent responses on these two plays, and both questions were equally popular. It is interesting to note that this text pairing’s popularity with centres is growing.
For both questions, responses were frequently informed by illuminating contextual discussion, and the best fruitfully compared the use of stagecraft, setting and dialogue across the two plays. Candidates were able to engage readily with the disturbing yet comical undertones of both Middleton’s and Orton’s texts and also grasped the importance of audience for these two plays. Critical views were on the whole judiciously selected, and in some cases the candidate’s autonomous reading of these plays was as sophisticated as the expert views quoted.
Those who chose Q10 generally agreed with the given statement, offering astute analysis of the bleakness and pessimism in both plays, but the strongest candidates also argued cogently for the dramatic impact of ‘creating opportunities for laughter’. One candidate noted that “both playwrights employ the conventions of farce which makes the audience complicit in the disturbing contents of each narrative, revealing our own ‘human nature’ to find comedy in what, perhaps, we should fear.”
a720u20-jun25-11-q: Q11 was also popular, with most candidates agreeing that hypocrisy is an obvious focus in both plays but also arguing that there is a great deal more than this in both plays. Religious hypocrisy was seen to dominate the discussion for many, but also the hypocrisy within social institutions and rituals and the hypocrisy of political institutions were examined. Some explored the relationship between power and hypocrisy, with focused discussion on the corruption of authority figures. One candidate observed: “Orton’s black farce dismantles the façade of the respectability of 1960’s England, reflecting the idea that institutions such as the police force are not pillars of order – which they should be – but rather agents of manipulation.”
a720u20-jun25-12-q:
Q12 appeared to be less popular than Q13, but both allowed candidates to make connections between the plays, as the issue of ‘domestic’ applies readily to both, as well as the idea of ‘the plays appealing to those with ‘social privilege’. Most argued that Wilde’s play is more obviously focused on a socially privileged society and directed towards a socially privileged audience of its time, but several saw the modern equivalents of appealing to the socially privileged in Betrayal, for example the significance of ‘squash’ and the holiday in Taormina. However, the most discerning argued that Pinter appears to criticise rather than to entertain, and the appeal of this play may be broader in scope than the Wilde play. The darker elements of Emma’s marriage were explored and the reverse chronology was discussed as an important contrast to Wilde’s dramatic techniques in Lady Windermere’s Fan.
While Lady Windermere is of course a lady of leisure with servants, many thought that her attention to the roses at the start of the play is enough indication of her ‘domestic’ role and significance, and the stronger responses argued that the word ‘domestic’ implies a less significant dramatic context, highly appropriate for a ‘comedy of manners’. In Betrayal, ‘domestic’ was seized upon more literally, with Emma’s attempts to improve the flat with various domestic symbols. There was plenty of pertinent discussion of dialogue as evidence of various social attitudes, and importantly many argued that the issues of women’s domination and exclusion by men make both plays serious vehicles for social messaging.
a720u20-jun25-13-q: Q13 gave free rein to those who wanted to write about gender equality in both plays, and most explored the dialogue and behaviour of key characters in depth and detail. Some approached the topic through a discussion about power and a popular view was that ‘women are unequal and submissive within society in both plays’. Most seemed to see Mrs Erlynne as the only female character with power and autonomy, while Agatha represented the opposite end of the spectrum. There was a strong focus on staging in both plays to illustrate gender inequality, with candidates frequently pointing that women have to secretly ‘listen in to men’ while hiding. The blunter dialogue by Robert and Jerry in Betrayal when Emma asks to join them in squash was seen as a harsher example of domineering and dismissive attitudes to women, while others delighted in exploring the more subtle and nuanced satirical dialogue of Lady Windermere’s Fan. Overall, it was encouraging to see genre-based discussion of both plays informing central arguments, with candidates using sound literary contextual knowledge to develop their connections.
a720u20-jun25-14-q:
As noted in previous reports, very few centres study this pairing. However, those who do study these plays clearly enjoy the opportunity to discuss the power of different social contexts and the social issues which arise in close comparative study. There were several very focused and ably argued responses to the idea of ‘what needs radical reform’ in Q14, and many concentrated on the abuse of power in law and justice departments / institutions and the need for society to break down intolerance and prejudice as an important starting point. Strong cases were made for the dramatic use of the female characters, with one very able candidate observing “Both female idealists, Irina and Isabella, highlight the ingrained corruption within both societies, but pose a threat to its ability to occur by forcefully opposing societal failures.”
A very small minority attempted Q15, but their main focus in discussing the ‘presentation of morality’ was appropriately on the individuals in whom the audiences see the embodiment of virtue or vice. As noted in previous reports, the standard of discussion on these texts was consistently high, with most candidates showing an impressive grasp of concepts and issues, as well as their social contexts and a keen appreciation of the plays’ stagecraft and characterisation.
Summary of key points • Candidates should think carefully about all aspects of an essay question and should make sure they are fully engaged with the explicit focus in the question. • There is no need for over-long notes and plans which detract from the time available to develop a good argument. • Shorter sentences should be encouraged. Too many candidates are using one sentence paragraphs which ramble awkwardly and the examiner has to try to find the different points made. Please aim for coherence and cogency rather than quantity. • Contexts are only useful if they support the point made or are helpful to the discussion of the question. Sweeping, uninformed statements about how people were treated in various time periods are of little consequence without specific examples. Candidates are now better at using literary / cultural material for contexts, and this is to be encouraged. • Avoid using critical views if they are not relevant or especially if they are fabricated. There must be evidence of purposeful use. • All candidates should use their time wisely and ensure that all tasks they are required to do on this paper are attempted. It is not sensible to leave out the Shakespeare extract question, and we encourage candidates to start with this in Section A, as it is intended to be a helpful stimulus for the Shakespeare essay. Leaving this question to the end is unhelpful to both candidate and examiner, as when scripts are scanned the detachment of this task from the rest of the section response can be problematic. • Finally, we ask all candidates to try to improve the legibility of their handwriting and not to use gel pens as instructed on the front of the paper. This year was more challenging than usual, with a higher number of scripts which were extremely difficult to read. Examiners should not have to guess a word. Marks will undoubtedly be compromised if the clarity of the script is seriously impaired. If a candidate has a real problem with being able to write clearly, it is advisable to submit a request to word process the script instead

a720u20-oct20-01-i:
As in previous series, the Shakespeare extract question exposed a lack of textual knowledge. Their evident unfamiliarity with the extract caused some candidates to struggle to understand the import of the given speeches and seriously hampered their attempt to analyse successfully Shakespeare’s use of language and imagery. The more successful responses selected pertinent imagery and other uses of language from the extract which directly related to the given question focus (AO2). Weaker responses floundered at understanding key lines in the speeches and also featured errors in concepts and terminology (AO1).
It is a matter of some concern that AO3 seems to be neglected and marginalised in some candidate responses, despite its double weighting for the Shakespeare essay task. Too many broad-brush references are made to history and perceived social attitudes, with little relevance to the question or indeed the text. It is far better to focus on cultural concepts and ideas and literary traditions and background in trying to find rich contextual material. The strongest responses in this section were on The Tempest, a trend which was apparent in 2019 also.
For AO5, it is pleasing to note an improved effort to draw on and integrate relevant interpretations, including critical views into the candidate’s argument.

a720u20-oct20-08-q:
Question 8 on The Duchess of Malfi and A Streetcar Named Desire was the most popular question in Section B, and some candidates focused on connections with reasonable success. Others showed some difficulty in making connections beyond a few superficial similarities. There was insufficient thought given in general to ‘ideas and constraints of her time’, and AO3 was addressed through token acknowledgements to the different eras, or simply through sweeping generalisations about history and politics. Question 12 on Lady Windermere’s Fan and Betrayal produced a few really good responses, showing sound knowledge of both plays and a firm grasp on the presentation of ‘secrecy and disguise’. Question 11 on The Revenger’s Tragedy and Loot was also well done, responses showing a genuine engagement with ‘the attack on family values’ and a clear enthusiasm for both plays.
Summary of key points
Where responses were successful, they generally featured:
• good knowledge and understanding of the text • appropriate support from and references to the play • a clear engagement with critical views, usually put to good purpose • attempts to integrate contextual materials (AO3) and other interpretations (AO5) to develop and support the central arguments in responses • generally accurate and coherent expression.
Where responses were less successful, they generally featured:
• insecure knowledge and understanding of the text, particularly in the extract question • poorly constructed sentences and paragraphs: it was common to see sentences which stretched to over half a page in the booklet and pages with no paragraphs • sweeping generalisations in discussing context/inaccurate historical referencing • failing to engage with the whole essay question.

Summary and Advice Component 3 was designed primarily to test candidates’ skills in creative reading and literary analysis. In addition, examples of contextual materials and critical readings are supplied to test candidates’ ability to understand and apply supporting materials which they have seen for the first time. Not only is this an effective way to examine A level candidates, it is also one of the ways Eduqas has responded to the regulator’s requirement to examine in different ways across the whole specification. Candidates who do not give due emphasis to AOs 1 and 2 in their responses but write extensively on pre-learned contextual materials instead subvert the purpose of the examination and fail to earn much of the credit that is available under the heavily weighted AOs. Candidates should:  give adequate time to close reading and fact checking before embarking on analysis – mistakes such as claiming that Mrs Ramsay is called Rose or that Lord Henry is a clergyman are unnecessary and damaging  offer a brief, supported overview in the introduction so as to confirm understanding and engagement with the arc of the extract  take account of the general features of the passage such as level of formality; tone; structure; narrative voice and use of direct speech and/or free indirect discourse - but do not offer these as stand-alone points – observations such as these are useful only as part of an analysis of the ways in which writers make meaning otherwise they remain simply labels
19  avoid or be very sparing with linguistic terminology – identifying features such as noun phrases, pre-modifiers or fronted adverbials do not, of themselves, contribute to creative engagement or literary analysis  take careful account of the supporting extracts in the course of writing rather than devoting separate sections of the essays to addressing AO3 and AO5  be very careful and sparing with the use of pre-learned contextual materials (see example above) and avoid assertion or distorting readings so as to accommodate irrelevant observations on contexts  in supporting critical analysis, make brief references to key words and phrases but do not copy out long passages of the text  study the WJEC online materials which deal with the appreciation of prose - should help candidates to distinguish descriptive writing or commentary from literary analysis.

Many of the responses to this poem relied upon description and paraphrase. In most cases a better planned answer which focused upon the subtle changes in tone and attitude would have been far more productive than the syllable counting and elaborate claims about the
20 significance of iambic pentameter which were much in evidence. This poem also has a lesson to teach about reading and re-reading so as to gain some grip upon: implicit meaning and attitudes; the effects of repetition; the language choices such as “murmur” or “mild refusal”; the use of imagery from painting, film and architecture and the significance of punctuation including the use of italics and dashes. There were quite a number who did look closely at these details and managed to score very well. Further to the point made in the overview about candidates bringing unsupported meanings to the poems rather than drawing them out, there were quite a few who spent time speculating about the sort of mistake which interested Fenton. Some wrote extensively (and without support) of the mistake he had made in choosing a partner; others suggested that he was in the wrong job (!) and was only now facing up to it. Unproductive writing of this sort damages both the sense of engagement and the coherence of candidates’ work.
Summary and Advice Candidates should:  recognise that unseen poetry requires very careful reading and re-reading before the nuances and complexities of the work become fully apparent – this has strong implications for time-management  as with the prose section, a brief and supported overview of the whole work confirms understanding and engagement  when making observations about the features of a poem always make these part of a point about how meaning is made or effects achieved otherwise this is simply naming of parts or feature-spotting  avoid any writing about contexts or suggestions about different ways of reading the poems because these AOs (3 and 5) are not rewarded  further to the above, understand the difference between analysing the ways a poet creates ambiguity (AO2) and discussing different interpretations (AO5 not rewarded here)  understand the difference between using what is commonly understood to be implied by a word or phrase (e.g. `scared’ and religion) and discussing the context of religion in detail  make good use of the online WJEC/Eduqas resources devoted to the practical criticism of poetry.
Examiners report on their excitement about this new component and the satisfaction experienced in marking the best responses. On the other hand, the first live run of an examination is bound to teach lessons (which have been discussed above) and it must be noted that examiners were surprised by the weight of unproductive contextual material and the formulaic approaches which candidates brought to this unseen paper. The message is that skills of literary analysis should be of primary concern when preparing candidates for Component 3; potted histories, biographies and rote learning of terminology should be placed firmly on the back burner.

In this passage there were some challenges to candidates’ understanding which needed close consideration and this is a very good example of material which requires careful re- reading and digesting before attempting a response. In order to appreciate the full impact of the passage, readers need to understand that the barman has fallen asleep drunk in his shoddy room after his lunchtime shift in the pub and before he begins his evening duties. This rumpled, frowsty picture of working life partly depends upon that context and it was alarming to see a significant number of candidates react to the idea of waking-up by suggesting that it was five o’clock in the morning and Bob was getting up before dawn for a day’s work. This is a mis-reading which seriously changes the meaning and diminishes the intended impact of the piece and brings into question those candidates’ engagement.
As in Q1, weaker responses were context-led and despite the care taken in stating Bob’s age at the top of the passage and the date of the novel’s publication, there were still many candidates who felt that the personal trauma of the First World War was the most significant factor in Bob’s alcoholism. Many of the same candidates felt that Ella’s light-hearted humming and “buoyant body” were the direct consequences of women gaining the vote which allowed them to go on to lengthy discussions of the Suffragette movement. Equally, Bob’s dream of the coast of Spain in 1929 was presented as evidence of his need for a holiday in the sun. Candidates need to be persuaded to interrogate a passage in the light of common sense as well as their broad historical knowledge.
The issue of unbalanced and excessive (often unconvincing) approaches to context was discussed in detail in last year’s report and colleagues are respectfully advised to take another look at that. For this year, suffice to say that broad and assertive writing on pre- learned contexts usually took up the time needed to analyse the style and techniques of this fascinating passage and produced some low-scoring responses.
At the other end of the spectrum some candidates made effective and convincing use of their knowledge and understanding of Modernism which, at its best, went beyond name- checking writers such as Joyce and Woolf and showed some genuine insight into new techniques illustrated by this passage. High quality essays also made constructive use of both extracts which had been chosen as examples of comment which could have been effective in addressing either or both AO3 and AO5 depending on how candidates chose to use them – a good number showed excellent judgement and understanding in this respect.
